# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- Berkshire County was established in **1761**, in far-western Massachusetts bordering both New York and Vermont — meaning a family in a border town there may have generated records in neighboring states too.

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**Civil registration**
- Massachusetts required town clerks to record vital events as early as 1639, but statewide centralized collection only began in **1841** (the first state in the nation to do so). Boston is excluded until 1850, but for Berkshire County, this means:
  - **1820–1840:** Records exist only at the **town level** — go to the town clerk, not a state office.
  - **1841–1850:** Events should also appear in the state-level system.
- **Marriage tip:** Intentions were commonly recorded in the *bride's* home town, with possible additional entries in the groom's town and their town of residence — check all three towns.

**Where to look online:**
- FamilySearch collection **"Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (collection ID 2061550) covers this period at the town level.
- Two **digitized but browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) volumes were also located:
  - **Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, Berkshire County, 1761–1850** (imageGroupNumber 004500891, 512 images) — must be browsed page by page.
  - **Pittsfield Congregational Church Records, 1791–1850** (imageGroupNumber 004500892, 274 images) — same limitation.

**Where to look physically:**
- Town/city clerk offices for each Berkshire County town hold the originals; contact them by mail or in person.

---

## Church Records

- **Denominations confirmed:** A Congregational church in Pittsfield is documented in the browse-only volume above. Other denominations (Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, etc.) were not confirmed in this survey.
- **Statewide coverage:** FamilySearch's **"Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (collection ID 1921657) includes other Berkshire County congregations where they survive.

---

## Probate Records

- **"Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"** (FamilySearch collection ID 1678901) spans this period.
- Originals are held at the **Berkshire County Probate Court** — contact them directly for records not yet digitized.

---

## Other Record Types

| Record Type | Collection / Notes |
|---|---|
| Federal Census (1820, 1830, 1840, 1850) | Search via Ancestry or FamilySearch census collections |
| Passenger Lists | "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (ID 1784312) — less likely for an inland family unless they emigrated overseas |
| Naturalization | "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (ID 1459213) |
| Land Records | Held at **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds**; no specific digitized collection was confirmed in this survey |
| Military Records | Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for service/pension files |
| Cemetery Records | Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers | Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices |

---

## Repository Quick Reference

| Repository | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Free | Multiple statewide collections listed above |
| Ancestry | Subscription | Best for federal census; also has vital and church collections |
| Find A Grave | Free | Cemetery/burial records |
| Newspapers.com | Subscription | Obituaries, announcements |
| Fold3 | Subscription | Military records |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Free (some online; some require request) | Federal military, immigration, naturalization |
| Town clerk offices (each Berkshire town) | In-person or mail | Originals of 1820–1841 vital records |
| Berkshire County Probate Court | In-person or mail | Wills, administrations, guardianships |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds | In-person or mail | Land records |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **For 1820–1840 vital events**, the town clerk is your first stop — no state-level filing existed yet. After 1841, check both the town and the state system.
2. **The two digitized Berkshire County volumes** (town vital records and Pittsfield Congregational church records) are online but require manual, page-by-page browsing — plan time for that.
3. **Because the family's town borders both New York and Vermont**, also search the adjoining counties in those states for vital, church, and land records. Families close to a state line commonly generated records on either side. The specific bordering New York and Vermont counties were not confirmed in this survey — a quick follow-up lookup to identify those counties by name is recommended before finalizing a search plan.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Massachusetts required town/city clerks to record births, marriages, and deaths as early as 1639 (not universally followed), and became the first state with a permanent **statewide** recording system in **1841** — Boston itself is excluded from the state system until 1850, per the FamilySearch Wiki ["Massachusetts Vital Records"](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records). output.text_response:
The locality guide for **Jalisco, Mexico (1880–1920)** has been produced and saved to the project (as `loc_001`).

Here's a summary of what it covers:

**Key Record Types**
- **Civil Registration** – Town-by-town birth and marriage registers, legally required from 1859 (strictly enforced after 1867). Digitized on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Catholic Parish Registers** – Baptisms, marriages, and burials from the Archdiocese of Guadalajara, also digitized at FamilySearch and Ancestry. Both sources should be searched together since they often record the same event differently.

**Critical Search Tips for a Two-Surname Family**
1. **Search each surname separately.** Most online indexes only index the father's surname, so searching both names together will cause records to be missed.
2. **Women retain their birth surname.** A married woman never takes her husband's name in Mexican records; always search her under her own birth family name.

**Important Caveats**
- Many record books are photographed but not fully indexed — some research will require browsing scanned images page by page rather than name-searching.
- Some original registers remain only on paper at local and state archives in Mexico, not yet accessible online.

The project is now ready for the next step: building a research plan or running searches using this guide as the jurisdictional foundation.

args.query: Jalisco Mexico civil registration genealogy records

quirks: Spanish double-surname system: paternal surname is usually first, maternal surname second; a woman keeps her maiden surname after marriage in Catholic, legal, and civil records (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Naming Customs, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Naming_Customs).

Most FamilySearch indexed records contain only the paternal (first) surname; when searching a person who used two surnames, search by the paternal surname alone, and also try a parent search using only each parent's first surname (FamilySearch Wiki, Improve your Search Results for Hispanic Ancestors, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org).

Civil registration (Registro Civil) was established by decree in 1859 but was not vigorously enforced until the republic was restored in 1867, so coverage for 1859-1867 is thin even though the law existed from 1859 (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

Both church and civil marriage records exist after 1859 - search both, since the Catholic Church kept parallel marriage records after civil registration began, and church weddings were often accepted locally even though the 1917 constitution required civil marriage for legal recognition (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

Civil registration in Jalisco is kept at the municipio level, not centrally - route record requests to the local civil registry office for the specific municipio (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

Divorce was not legal in Mexico until after the 1917 constitution, and divorce records are held by municipio courts, not the civil registry; FamilySearch's library holds very few of these (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

When a person cannot be found, search neighboring parishes/municipios as well, per standard Mexico church-and-civil search strategy (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Research Tips and Strategies, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Research_Tips_and_Strategies).

- **Formed:** Jalisco became the 9th state of Mexico on 23 December 1823 (FamilySearch Wiki, Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy).

- **Indigenous populations:** Two significant groups recorded for the state: the Huichol and the Nahua/Otomí communities (FamilySearch Wiki, Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy).
- **Religion:** Catholicism has been the primary religion for centuries nationally (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Getting Started, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Getting_Started).
- **Key administrative event for records:** The Registro Civil (civil registration) was established nationally by decree of President Benito Juárez on 28 July 1859, but vigorous enforcement did not begin until the republic was restored in 1867 (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

- Because most indexed FamilySearch records carry only the paternal surname, search first by paternal surname alone, then retry with the maternal surname alone, for a family known to have used two surnames (FamilySearch Wiki, Improve your Search Results for Hispanic Ancestors in FamilySearch.org, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org).

---

This survey covers Jalisco, Mexico, for the years 1880 to 1920, looking at the kinds of records that could document births and marriages for a family that used two surnames, a normal Mexican naming custom in which a child carries both the father's and mother's family names. The main sources are Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials), kept by the Archdiocese of Guadalajara and digitized by FamilySearch and Ancestry, and civil registration records kept town by town starting in 1859 (though not strictly enforced until 1867), also digitized at both of those sites; both kinds of records should be checked side by side since they often record the same event differently. Two warnings matter most: most online indexes only search by the father's surname, so searches should be tried with each surname separately rather than both together, and a married woman keeps her own birth surname in Mexican records rather than taking her husband's, so she should never be searched for under a different name. A large share of the old record books for this area have been photographed but not yet typed into a searchable index, so some searching will mean paging through scanned images rather than typing a name into a search box, and some original record books remain only on paper at local and state archives in Mexico rather than online anywhere.

Research planning for this family in Jalisco can proceed next using this guide.

quirks: Spanish double-surname system: paternal surname is usually first, maternal surname second; a woman keeps her maiden surname after marriage in Catholic, legal, and civil records (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Naming Customs, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Naming_Customs).

Most FamilySearch indexed records contain only the paternal (first) surname; when searching a person who used two surnames, search by the paternal surname alone, and also try a parent search using only each parent's first surname (FamilySearch Wiki, Improve your Search Results for Hispanic Ancestors, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org).

Civil registration (Registro Civil) was established by decree in 1859 but was not vigorously enforced until the republic was restored in 1867, so coverage for 1859-1867 is thin even though the law existed from 1859 (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

Both church and civil marriage records exist after 1859 - search both, since the Catholic Church kept parallel marriage records after civil registration began, and church weddings were often accepted locally even though the 1917 constitution required civil marriage for legal recognition (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

Civil registration in Jalisco is kept at the municipio level, not centrally - route record requests to the local civil registry office for the specific municipio (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

Divorce was not legal in Mexico until after the 1917 constitution, and divorce records are held by municipio courts, not the civil registry; FamilySearch's library holds very few of these (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

When a person cannot be found, search neighboring parishes/municipios as well, per standard Mexico church-and-civil search strategy (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Research Tips and Strategies, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Research_Tips_and_Strategies).

No tool result in this survey identified any specific destroyed or lost record set for Jalisco civil registration or Catholic church records in 1880-1920. The FamilySearch Wiki's Mexico Civil Registration page states generally that early civil registration (1859-1867) was thinly enforced nationally, which is a coverage/enforcement gap rather than a record loss (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration). ## Research tips

- Search both the civil registration and the parallel Catholic church marriage/baptism/burial record for the same event — both exist after 1859 and often disagree or fill each other's gaps (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

- Work outward from one found record: find the ancestor's birth, then siblings' births, then the parents' marriage (which often names the grandparents), then the parents' own birth records, repeating for both lines (FamilySearch Wiki, Mexico Civil Registration "Strategy" section).

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim (Bushmills area), 1780–1870

## Jurisdiction Note
The place-lookup tool returned no matches for Billy, Antrim, or Ireland in this session, so collection counts and place-specific catalog hits came back empty. The Church of Ireland records page loaded directly and is the basis for the church records section. Everything in this guide that was not returned by a tool is flagged as unconfirmed.

---

## Civil Registration
Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths **did not begin in Ireland until 1864**. For the 1780–1870 target window, only the final six years (1864–1870) fall within civil registration. Prior to 1864, church registers are the primary source.

- **Post-1864 records held at:** General Register Office for Northern Ireland (GRONI)

---

## Church Records

### Church of Ireland
The *Ireland Church Records* FamilySearch Wiki page confirms that Church of Ireland registers began in 1536 but **two-thirds were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office of Ireland fire in Dublin**. Whether Billy parish's specific registers survived is **not confirmed** by this session's tool results — this is the most important outstanding question.

**To verify survival:**
- Check the **RCB Library's** (Representative Church Body) parish-register list:
  [RCB Parish Registers PDF](https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf)
- Query **PRONI's Church Records Guide** for what they hold on microfilm or original:
  [PRONI Guide to Church Records](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf)
  [PRONI Digitised Church Records](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1)

### Presbyterian Church
North Antrim/Bushmills was a heavily Presbyterian area. The same FamilySearch page notes Presbyterian registers mostly date from the 1600s but the **average starting date is 1830**. PRONI holds many Presbyterian registers for County Antrim.

### Catholic Records
Catholics were approximately 40% of the broader Irish population in 1861; the Bushmills/north Antrim area was historically more Protestant. Catholic registers generally begin later and are held at PRONI or the National Library of Ireland.

### Substitute Sources for Register Losses
If Church of Ireland registers are destroyed, the **Betham**, **Crossle**, and **Thrift Genealogical Abstracts** (available on FindMyPast) provide substitute coverage.

---

## Census Records
Most 19th-century Irish census returns before 1901 were destroyed (widely reported but **not confirmed by a tool result this session**). No Antrim-specific census collection was returned by the catalog/collection tools.

---

## Land & Probate Records
Not confirmed by a tool result this session. Generally, PRONI holds Northern Irish land and probate records; the National Archives of Ireland holds national-level records.

---

## Record Losses
- **1922 PROI fire:** Destroyed roughly two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers nationally. Billy parish's survival status is unconfirmed — check the RCB Library list directly.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What They Hold | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **RCB Library** (Church of Ireland), Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14 | Surviving Church of Ireland parish registers | library@ireland.anglican.org |
| **PRONI**, 2 Titanic Boulevard, Belfast BT3 9HQ | Church records (microfilm/original) for Northern Ireland, incl. north Antrim; civil/court/land records | proni@communities-ni.gov.uk; 028 9053 4800 |
| **National Archives / National Library of Ireland**, Dublin | National-level records, pre-1922 copies | mail@nationalarchives.ie |

---

## Key Next Steps
1. **Check the RCB Library's parish register list** for Billy parish to find whether its Church of Ireland registers for 1780–1870 survived 1922 and from what start date.
2. **Consult PRONI's church-records guide** to see what PRONI holds on microfilm for Billy parish.
3. **Search PRONI's online digitized church records** for any Billy parish holdings already online.
4. For pre-1864 non-church records (land, probate, court), query PRONI directly with the parish name.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, barony of Carey and barony of Lower Dunluce, Poor Law Union of Coleraine, County Antrim, Ulster.
- Contains the post town of **Bushmills** and part of Dunserverick.
- The Church of Ireland rectory/vicarage of Billy forms the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor. For Roman Catholic purposes, the parish is part of the **district of Coleraine**. Meeting houses existed for Presbyterians, Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists.
- After 1922, custody split between all-Ireland bodies (pre-partition) and Northern Ireland/PRONI/GRONI (post-partition) — the parish boundary itself did not change.

---

## Vital (Civil) Registration

| Event | Registration begins | Coverage for 1780–1870 |
|---|---|---|
| Births & Deaths | 1864 | Only 1864–1870 |
| Protestant marriages | 1845 | Only 1845–1870 |
| Catholic marriages | 1864 | Only 1864–1870 |

**Implication:** The years 1780–1863/1844 lie **entirely before civil registration** — church registers are the primary source for the bulk of this period.

---

## Church Records (The Core Gap-Filling Need)

### What was found online
| Record | Date range | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ballylinny (Billy parish) Presbyterian/nonconformist christenings | 1837–1868 | FamilySearch image group 007907410_008_M9VF-SK5, 65 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed | Free |
| Ballylinny (Billy parish) marriages | 1837–1864 | FamilySearch image group 007765074_009_M9VX-Q7W, 50 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed | Free |

### Known gaps
- **1780–1836** is not covered by any confirmed digitized register.
- Church of Ireland, Catholic, Methodist, and Covenanter registers for Billy parish itself have no confirmed online holdings — they are unconfirmed online, not necessarily absent.
- Two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers nationally were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office of Ireland fire; it is not confirmed whether Billy's own Church of Ireland registers survived.

---

## Repositories and Indexes to Close Church-Register Gaps

### Online
| Repository | Relevant collections | Gap it closes | URL |
|---|---|---|---|
| **National Library of Ireland** | Free digitized Catholic parish-register scans (Catholic district of Coleraine covers Billy) | Catholic baptisms, marriages, burials | https://registers.nli.ie/ — free |
| **FamilySearch** | Ballylinny volumes above; also full-text search engine for unindexed registers | Use FTS for the unindexed Ballylinny volumes | https://www.familysearch.org — free |
| **Ancestry** | Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655–1915; Diocese and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes, 1623–1866; Abstracts of Wills and Marriages, 1620–1923 | Catholic registers; marriage license/probate substitutes | https://www.ancestry.com — subscription |
| **FindMyPast** | Irish Parish Register Baptisms/Marriages/Burials; Ffolliott Collection; Ireland Non-Conformist Births/Marriages/Burials; Irish Quaker Collection; Betham/Crossle/Thrift Genealogical Abstracts | Church of Ireland, nonconformist, Quaker; pre-1922-fire probate/marriage substitutes | https://search.findmypast.com — subscription |
| **Ulster Historical Foundation** | County Antrim church-register indexing project | Fills index gaps for registers not yet name-indexed elsewhere | http://www.ancestryireland.com — subscription |
| **RootsIreland.ie** | County-level Irish parish register transcription index | Antrim parishes not in FamilySearch's indexed set | http://www.rootsireland.ie — subscription |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Address | Holdings / Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)** | 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ; proni@communities-ni.gov.uk; +44 28 9053 4800 | Original/microfilm church registers for Ulster parishes; may hold Billy parish Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, and other registers not yet digitized — **first stop for unconfirmed registers** |
| **RCB Library (Church of Ireland)** | Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735; library@ireland.anglican.org; +353 1 492 3979 | Church of Ireland parish registers; published List of Parish Registers shows what survives for each parish and where it is held | https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy |
| **National Archives of Ireland** | Bishop Street, Dublin D08 DF85; mail@nationalarchives.ie | National-level records to 1922, genealogy guides | http://www.nationalarchives.ie |
| **National Library of Ireland** | Kildare Street, Dublin D02 P638 | Catholic register scans (also free online at registers.nli.ie) | http://www.nli.ie |

---

## Other Record Types

### Land (Census Substitutes)
- **Tithe Applotment Books** (1820s): tax paid to the established church — identifies householders by townland; use as a census substitute.
- **Griffith's Valuation** (1840s): a Valuation Office survey. A digitized volume for Ballylinny, Billy (VAL 12B/1/7B), dated 1867–1881, exists on FamilySearch (image group 004689599, browse-only, not indexed).

### School Records
- **Deffrick National School Girls** (V. 239-240), Billy parish, 1 Apr 1867 – 11 Sep 1933 — FamilySearch image group 008682995_005_M94W-68Y, 50 images (browse-only, unindexed). Tail end only falls in target period.

### Probate
- Pre-1858 probate was handled by diocesan courts; most originals destroyed in the 1922 PRO fire. Use substitute abstracts: **Betham, Crossle, and Thrift Genealogical Abstracts** (FindMyPast) and the **Ireland, Indexes to Wills, 1591–1866** (Ancestry).

### Census
- 1821–1851 censuses were largely destroyed; 1861/1871 were destroyed by government order. No Billy-specific census material was found. Use Tithe Applotment and Griffith's Valuation instead.

---

## Known Record Losses
- Two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers nationally were destroyed in the 1922 PRO fire; Billy's own status is unconfirmed.
- Most pre-1858 Irish probate records were destroyed in the same fire.
- Irish censuses for 1861 and 1871 were destroyed by government order; earlier census survivals are fragmentary.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the NLI Catholic register scans** (free, registers.nli.ie) for the Catholic district of Coleraine to cover Billy's Catholic families before 1864.
2. **Contact PRONI directly** about Billy parish's Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist, and Covenanter registers — many Ulster registers are held there but not yet digitized.
3. **Use FamilySearch full-text search** for the two unindexed Ballylinny volumes (christenings and marriages, 1837–1868) — search by surname keyword rather than the standard name index.
4. **Ulster Presbyterian registers** in Antrim average a start date of c.1830 — expect limited coverage for the meeting houses in Billy before that date.
5. **Catholic registers** often began only after 1828 (Catholic Emancipation) in rural Ulster — gap before that date is normal.
6. **Catholic parish boundaries ≠ civil parish boundaries** — a family's Catholic entries may sit under a neighbouring parish name in the district of Coleraine records.
7. **Tithe Applotment (1820s) and Griffith's Valuation (1840s)** are the best tools for locating families by townland before 1864; use them to anchor a household before searching church registers.
8. **Surrounding parishes** should be searched in parallel, as Church of Ireland and Catholic ecclesiastical territories regularly crossed civil-parish lines.

# Christ Church, Philadelphia — Original 1734 Marriage Register

## Where Is the Original Held?

The original 1734 marriage register is almost certainly held by **Christ Church itself (its parish archives)**, not a government office or diocesan repository. Here's why:

- **Pennsylvania had no civil marriage registration until 1913.** A 1734 marriage was recorded only by the church — there is no county or state equivalent to look for.
- **Christ Church is still an active Episcopal congregation** (founded 1682, still operating today). The FamilySearch Wiki on Pennsylvania Church Records states that for Episcopal churches, **the Diocese of Pennsylvania only receives records from closed congregations**. Since Christ Church is still active, its old registers stay with the parish.
- **The Historical Society of Pennsylvania** holds *abstracts* (derivative summaries) of various Pennsylvania church records — useful for confirming a marriage exists, but **not** the original handwritten register.

## What Was Found Online

No digitized image or online transcription of the Christ Church 1734 marriage register was located in this survey. It does not appear to be on FamilySearch's image viewer. The compiled/derivative indexes on FamilySearch — *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* and *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* — may index an entry if one exists, but would not give you access to the original volume.

## How to Access the Original

1. **Contact Christ Church, Philadelphia directly** — reach out to their parish archives or rector's office to ask about in-person viewing or requesting a copy of the 1734 register.
2. **Search the FamilySearch indexes first** to confirm the entry and collect exact names and dates before you write to the church.
3. **Do not assume the Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds the original** — their collection is abstracts only.

## Important Caveats

No tool result in this survey confirms the precise shelf, room, or archive where the 1734 volume sits today. The statement that it resides with the parish is based on the general rule for active Episcopal congregations per the FamilySearch Wiki — the specific custodianship of this particular volume is unconfirmed beyond that.

# Locality Guide: The Alabama Region, c. 1800 (Pre-Statehood)

**Note on jurisdiction:** Depending on exactly where in present-day Alabama your ancestor lived, the records will be filed under one of two very different trails:

- **Interior/northern Alabama** (most of the region): part of the **Mississippi Territory**, a U.S. territory from 1798–1817, which became the separate **Alabama Territory** in 1817, then the State of Alabama in 1819.
- **The Mobile area** (far south): still under **Spanish colonial administration** until 1813, having passed from France (1702–1763) to Britain (1763–1780) to Spain (1780–1813).

Narrowing down where your ancestor lived is the most critical first step.

---

## Boundary Changes
| Period | Jurisdiction |
|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French colonial Mobile District |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish Mobile District |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory (inland Alabama) |
| 1813 | U.S. seizes Mobile from Spain |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory |
| 1819 | Alabama statehood |

---

## Available Record Types

### Census / Territorial Enumerations
- The Mississippi Territory took censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama — held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery**.
- FamilySearch has an **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** collection (overlaps the tail of your period at 1810) — useful as a census substitute.

### Land & Property Records
- A digitized but **browse-only** (0% name-indexed) FamilySearch volume: **"Territorial court and land records," Alabama, 1808–1819** (image group 004512889, 214 images) — directly in-period but must be browsed image by image.
- A second browse-only volume: **"County deed and probate records, Washington, Alabama, 1803–1820"** (image group 004512890, 96 images). Washington County was the first county organized in this part of the Mississippi Territory — a key in-period source.

### Probate Records
- FamilySearch: **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (begins nearly at the start of your window).
- The Washington County volume above also covers probate, 1803–1820.

### Church Records
- FamilySearch: **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** — in-period from 1803.
- For the Mobile area, **Catholic sacramental registers** from the Spanish era may be the earliest church source; these would be held at the Archdiocese of Mobile or in Spanish colonial archives.

### Marriage Records
- FamilySearch: **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** — the earliest marriage collection found, beginning just at the period's end.

### Colonial-Era Records (Mobile Area Only)
- French colonial records: **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence** (France), with microfilm copies at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**.
- Spanish colonial records (census returns, church registers, land grants): **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress**.

---

## Repository Guide

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (Montgomery) | Mississippi Territory censuses 1801–1810; territorial court, land, and probate originals |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish Mobile District records |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Original French colonial records |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District |
| NARA (National Archives) | Federal territorial, land office, and military records |

### Online (FamilySearch)
| Collection | Period |
|---|---|
| Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 | 1809+ |
| Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 | 1809+ |
| Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 | 1803+ |
| Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 | 1810+ |
| Territorial court/land records (browse only, image group 004512889) | 1808–1819 |
| Washington Co. deed/probate records (browse only, image group 004512890) | 1803–1820 |

---

## Records NOT Online
The Mississippi Territory censuses (1801/1805/1808/1810) and the Spanish/French colonial originals are **not available online** — these exist only in the physical repositories listed above. The two digitized FamilySearch volumes are online as images only, with no name index and no full-text search capability.

## Known Record Losses
No specific record losses for this place and period were confirmed by this survey. The thin online coverage reflects that much of what exists for 1798–1820 is simply **undigitized or held only in physical archives** — not necessarily destroyed.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Pin down the specific location first** — the Mississippi Territory vs. Spanish Mobile District distinction determines which archive and even which country's archive holds the records.
2. **Start with ADAH** (Alabama Department of Archives and History) for the Mississippi Territory censuses (1801–1810) and territorial court/land records, since FamilySearch's digitized copies are unindexed and must be browsed page by page.
3. **If near Mobile**, pursue the Spanish/French colonial trail (Archivo General de Indias in Seville; Library of Congress copies; Mobile Municipal Archives microfilm) rather than only Mississippi Territory sources.
4. **FamilySearch collections** starting in 1803–1809 (marriages, probate, church records) are the best online starting point and overlap your period.
5. For military service (War of 1812, Creek War 1813–14), check **NARA directly** for pension and bounty-land files.
6. No Alabama-specific vital records start date could be confirmed for this era; church, court, and territorial records are the practical substitutes for civil registration in 1800.

I looked into what kinds of old records survive for the Alabama region around the year 1800, when it was not yet its own state. At that time the area was split between the U.S.-run Mississippi Territory (covering most of inland Alabama) and, in the Mobile area only, Spanish colonial rule (following earlier French and British control) — so where your ancestor actually lived changes which archive holds the records. The most useful surviving pieces found were early territorial censuses and court/land/probate records held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, plus a couple of digitized but unindexed record books on FamilySearch that have to be flipped through page by page rather than searched by name; if your ancestor was near Mobile, the trail instead leads to Spanish records copied at the Library of Congress or held in Seville, Spain. One important warning: this survey could not find Alabama's own FamilySearch research guide pages working properly, so some details (like exactly when official birth/death recordkeeping began) remain unconfirmed and would need a direct look at the FamilySearch Wiki or the Alabama archives.

Narrowing down the specific county or settlement your ancestor lived in would be the most useful next step, since it determines which of these two very different record trails (Mississippi Territory vs. Spanish Mobile) to pursue first.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period, 1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The territory had no "Arkansas" civil jurisdiction in this period. It was part of **Spanish Louisiana from 1763** (when Spain received it from France by the Treaty of Paris) until it was secretly re-ceded to France in 1800, ahead of the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. The only organized European settlement was **Arkansas Post**, established as a French settlement in 1686 and continued under Spanish administration after 1763.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(Primary source for this period)*
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic — French and Spanish missionary priests maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials of both European settlers and Native Americans.
- **Online:** One digitized volume of **Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763–1800** is on FamilySearch (image group 008814402, 64 images). **Important caveats:** it is in Spanish, has **no name index**, and is **browse-only** — you must read it page by page.
- **Physical copies:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (originals) and Arkansas History Commission (transcriptions).

### Census / Population Records
- Spanish colonial administration kept periodic population counts ("padrones"), but **no digitized or indexed version was found** for this period.
- Likely physical-only at the repositories below, if extant.

### Land Records
- Land was distributed as Spanish colonial concessions/grants.
- Held at the **Arkansas History Commission**, the **Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain)**, and on **microfilm at the Library of Congress**.
- None found online in this survey.

### Military / Administrative Records
- Arkansas Post was a Spanish military post; records include military administrative documents.
- Likely held only at the **Archivo General de Indias** or on Library of Congress microfilm — not found online.

### Civil Vital Registration
- **None existed** in this period. Vital events were captured only in sacramental church registers.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What's There | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Spanish Colonial Sacramental Register, Arkansas Post, 1763–1800 (image group 008814402) | Browse-only, in Spanish, no name index |

> **Note:** Indexed FamilySearch collections for Arkansas (marriages, census substitutes, Freedmen's Bureau) begin in 1819–1837 — **none cover the Spanish period.**

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) | Transcribed colonial civil/military records and church-register transcriptions |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original sacramental registers from Arkansas Post |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) | Spanish colonial administrative originals: land concessions, military/civil records |
| Library of Congress | Microfilm copies of Spanish colonial Arkansas records |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search by settlement, not county.** FamilySearch's place system only resolves "Arkansas" to the state formed in 1836. Target *Arkansas Post* and *Spanish Louisiana* administrative sources specifically.

2. **Budget time for the unindexed church register.** The one digitized record (FamilySearch image group 008814402) is in Spanish with no name search — plan to browse it image by image.

3. **Plan across multiple repositories.** Originals and transcriptions are split between Little Rock (Arkansas History Commission, Diocese of Little Rock) and Seville (Archivo General de Indias), with microfilm at the Library of Congress. No single repository holds everything.

4. **Consider writing to archives directly.** Most records from this period have not been digitized or indexed, so written requests to the Arkansas History Commission and the Catholic Diocese of Little Rock are likely necessary.

---

## Records NOT Online

Spanish colonial civil/military administrative records, land concessions, and population counts (padrones) for Arkansas Post are not available in any online database found in this survey. The apparent absence online reflects a **digitization gap**, not confirmed record loss.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Spanish colonial period, 1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The territory had no "Arkansas" civil jurisdiction in this period. It was part of Spanish Louisiana from 1763 (when Spain received it from France by the Treaty of Paris) until Spain secretly re-ceded it to France in 1800, ahead of the 1803 Louisiana Purchase (Wikipedia, "Arkansas"). `place_search` only resolves "Arkansas" to the state formed in 1836 (`dateRange: "+1836/"`); there is no standardPlace for the Spanish-era jurisdiction, and `place_population` returned no data for 1763–1800 under that standardPlace.
- **Administrative/settlement center:** Arkansas Post, established as a French settlement in 1686 and continued under Spanish administration after 1763 — the only organized European settlement in the area during this period (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki "Arkansas Genealogy," Colonial Records section).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Spanish Louisiana (governed from New Orleans), reporting ultimately to colonial Spain.
- **Key historical events:** Transfer of the territory from France to Spain (1763), secret retrocession to France (1800), then the Louisiana Purchase (1803) bringing it under the United States.

## Boundary changes
- No county or state-level boundary history applies before 1800 — the only organized locus was the Arkansas Post garrison/settlement itself. "Arkansas County, Arkansas" as a civil jurisdiction postdates this period; records from the Spanish era are catalogued today under "Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas, United States" as a modern place label applied retroactively (see `volume_search` result below), not evidence that the county existed at the time.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide or county civil registration existed in this period; Arkansas's own civil vital registration is far later and outside this window. The FamilySearch Wiki's generic vital-records guidance (fetched for this survey) states only that "start dates vary by jurisdiction" and does not give an Arkansas-specific date — treat that as uncited for this place.
- **What exists:** Civil vital events were instead recorded in Spanish administrative and sacramental records at the post (see Church records).
- **Where held:** See Church records and the Repository guide below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic — French and Spanish missionary priests maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy," Church Records section).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials, recording both European settlers and Native Americans.
- **Where held:** Surviving registers are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, with transcribed copies at the Arkansas History Commission (FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy"). `volume_search` additionally located one digitized volume of "Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)" covering Arkansas Post, 1763–1800 (image group 008814402, 64 images, in Spanish). It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — **browse-only, and in Spanish**, so the researcher must read the original-language images page by page with no name search.
- **Gaps:** No separate online index for this register was found.
- **Language:** Spanish (and likely some French for the earlier portion of the register series, per the pre-1763 French mission tradition, though that is outside this period).

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** None — the first U.S. federal census reaching this area postdates the period.
- **State/provincial census:** Spanish colonial administration kept periodic population counts ("padrones") at the post as part of civil/military administration (FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy," Colonial Records section). No digitized or indexed version of a padrón was located by `collections_search` or `volume_search` for this period.
- **Access:** Not found online in this survey; likely physical-only, if extant, at the repositories below.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial administration at Arkansas Post would have generated land concessions and military/civil administrative records rather than a separate probate court system as later understood.
- **Where held:** Not identified by any tool in this survey as a distinct holding; see Land records and Repository guide.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land was granted by Spanish colonial authority (land concessions issued under Spanish administration), per the FamilySearch Wiki's Colonial Records note.
- **Types:** Land concessions/grants.
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch Wiki states Spanish colonial records — including land concessions — are held at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain, and in microfilm at the Library of Congress (FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy," Colonial Records section). No catalog or volume hit in this survey confirms a specific land-grant volume; treat this as the Wiki's claim, not independently confirmed by `catalog_search` (0 hits) or `volume_search`.

### Military records
- **Relevant context:** Arkansas Post was a Spanish military post; its records include military administrative records, per the Wiki's Colonial Records note, but no specific service or muster record set was located online.
- **Where held:** Likely only at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) or in Library of Congress microfilm, per the Wiki citation above; not independently confirmed by catalog or volume search.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not applicable in the modern sense for this period and place — there was no port-of-entry immigration-processing system; settlers arrived via French/Spanish colonial administrative channels, not documented port manifests.

### Other record types
- No school, tax, newspaper, or cemetery records were located for this period; none of the surveyed tools returned anything for these categories in this place/time window.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | One digitized (browse-only, unindexed) volume of Spanish Colonial Sacramental Registers for Arkansas Post, 1763–1800, image group 008814402 | Spanish-language church register of baptisms/marriages/burials | Free, browse-only (no name index) |

`collections_search` for "Arkansas" returned only three indexed collections (Arkansas County Marriages 1837–1957; Freedmen's Bureau Field Office Records 1865–1872; Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1819–1870) — **none overlap the 1763–1800 Spanish period**, confirming a coverage gap for this window on FamilySearch's indexed side. `catalog_search` for "Arkansas, United States" returned zero hits, a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist. `external_links_search` for Arkansas returned only generic national-level links (Ancestry's general census collection, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) with nothing specific to the Spanish colonial period.

**Coverage of this survey:** Only one digitized volume matched this place and period in `volume_search`; this is reported as the complete first-page result (`totalResults: 1`), not a partial sample.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) | Transcribed Spanish colonial civil/military records and church-register transcriptions, per the FamilySearch Wiki | In-person or written request |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from Arkansas Post | Written request to diocesan archives |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) | Spanish colonial administrative originals (land concessions, military/civil records) | In-person or written request (Spain) |
| Library of Congress | Microfilm copies of Spanish colonial Arkansas records | In-person or interlibrary loan request |

## Records NOT online
Spanish colonial civil/military administrative records, land concessions, and any population counts (padrones) for Arkansas Post are not available in any online database surveyed here. The one church-register volume that is online is unindexed images only.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that any specific Arkansas Post Spanish-era record series was destroyed or lost. Treat the apparent absence of civil/military and land records online as a digitization gap, not a confirmed loss, since no cited source states loss.

## Research tips
- This period predates any Arkansas civil jurisdiction as FamilySearch's place system models it (`place_search` resolves "Arkansas" only to the 1836 state), so searches must target "Arkansas Post" and Spanish Louisiana administrative sources, not a county-level 18th-century search.
- The one surviving digitized church register (image group 008814402) is in Spanish and not indexed — budget time to read it page by page rather than searching by name.
- Because the Wiki states originals/transcriptions are split between Little Rock (Arkansas History Commission, Diocese of Little Rock) and Seville (Archivo General de Indias), with microfilm at the Library of Congress, plan research across all three rather than assuming one repository holds everything (FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy," Colonial Records section).
- The generic FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched for "getting started," "online records," and "research tips" at the state level returned only template-level, non-Arkansas-specific content; they did not yield period-specific guidance, so this survey does not treat anything from them as an Arkansas claim.

---
This survey looked at Arkansas Post, the single Spanish colonial-era settlement in what is now Arkansas, for the years 1763 to 1800, when the region was ruled by Spain as part of Spanish Louisiana. The main surviving records are Catholic church registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials, kept at the time by missionary priests; one such register has been digitized by FamilySearch but is in Spanish, has no name index, and must be read page by page, while related land, military, and population records appear to survive mainly as originals in Little Rock, in Seville, Spain, and on microfilm at the Library of Congress rather than online. Because records from this period are organized around the small settlement of Arkansas Post rather than any modern Arkansas county, and most of what survives has not been digitized or indexed, this research will likely require written requests to the Arkansas History Commission, the Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, and potentially Spanish archives.

The next step is to decide whether to move to building a research plan around these repositories, most likely starting with the one digitized Arkansas Post church register.

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (around 1790)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Ohio did not yet exist as a jurisdiction in 1790. The governing authority was the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. **Washington County** was organized in 1788 (the first county) and **Hamilton County** in 1790. Two distinct land-grant systems operated in the territory:
- **Virginia Military District** — metes-and-bounds survey, for Virginia Revolutionary War veterans
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** — gridded survey, in northeastern Ohio

## Boundary Changes

- The Northwest Territory (1787) originally covered present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota.
- Further county splits continued throughout the period — you must identify **which county held jurisdiction at the specific date of your ancestor's event**, not assume today's county lines.
- Ohio became a state only in **1803** — records before that date are **territorial**, filed under the Northwest Territory or its organized counties.

---

## Available Records

### Land Records
- Virginia Military District warrants held at the **Virginia State Library**; Connecticut Western Reserve records at the **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland).
- **Online:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (FamilySearch collection 1542187, indexed). Also a browse-only volume of **Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799** (image group 005112233, 51 images, no name index — must be browsed page by page).

### Marriage / Church Records
- No statewide vital registration existed before 1803. Best substitutes:
  - **"Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013"** (FamilySearch collection 1803785) — reaches back into the territorial period.
  - **"Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950"** (FamilySearch collection 2246917) — the primary substitute for missing early birth and death records.

### Birth & Death Records
- **No dedicated online collection covers this period.** The nearest death collection ("Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001") starts well after 1803. This is a confirmed gap; church registers are the best available substitute.

### Census Records
- The 1790 federal census did **not** enumerate the Northwest Territory as settled states were — no 1790 schedule exists for Ohio. No territorial census for this window was found.

### Tax Records (Census substitute)
- **"Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"** (FamilySearch collection 1987542) — begins at statehood's edge.
- **Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803** (image group 005112240, 73 images, 12% indexed) — a genuine territorial-era substitute for the missing census.

### Probate & Court Records
- No online collection found for this period. Original records survive at **county courthouses** (Washington, Hamilton, etc.) and the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus — physical access only.

### Military Records
- No specific collection found for this window online. Service, pension, and bounty-land records are held at the **National Archives**.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1787–1950; County Marriages 1789–2013; Land Records 1787–1840; Tax Records 1800–1850; Washington County Tax 1799–1803; Territorial Land Records 1788–1799 | Free |
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus) | Early territorial court and land records | In-person / written request |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District land warrants | In-person / written request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person / written request |
| County Courthouses (Washington, Hamilton, etc.) | Original deed, probate, and court books | In-person / mail request |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military service, pensions, federal records | Free (finding aids) |

---

## Known Gaps
- **No 1790s census** survives for Ohio/Northwest Territory.
- **Early vital registration** (births, deaths) does not exist — church registers are the substitute.
- **Probate and court records** from this period are not online; physical courthouse or Ohio History Connection visits are required.
- No confirmed record *destruction* was identified — these are access/digitization gaps, not losses.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Identify the correct county first.** Washington (from 1788) and Hamilton (from 1790) are the starting points, but boundary changes were frequent — confirm which county held jurisdiction for the date and location of your ancestor's event.
2. **Know which land district applies.** Virginia Military District ancestors → Virginia State Library. Connecticut Western Reserve ancestors → Western Reserve Historical Society. These are entirely separate record systems.
3. **Use church records as your vital-record substitute.** Collection 2246917 (FamilySearch) starts in 1787 and is the best available source for births, deaths, and marriages where civil registration didn't yet exist.
4. **Use tax lists as your census substitute.** The Washington County Tax Records (1799–1803) and the Ohio Tax Records collection (from 1800) fill the gap left by the missing territorial census.
5. **Search the FamilySearch Catalog and the Ohio History Connection's own finding aids directly** — the catalog search returned no hits in this survey, suggesting a digitization gap rather than an absence of records.

---

**In plain terms:** In 1790, Ohio wasn't yet Ohio — it was the sparsely settled Northwest Territory, divided into a handful of early counties. Regular census-taking and civil vital registration didn't apply here yet, so surviving records are thin. Your best bets are church registers (available from 1787 online), early land records tied to two special grant zones with their own archives, and tax lists from just around 1800. Most court and estate records from this period survive only on paper at county courthouses or in Columbus. Knowing which early county had authority over your ancestor's location — and whether they were in the Virginia Military District or Connecticut Western Reserve — is the essential first step before any search.

Two distinct land-grant systems operated in the territory and matter for records: the **Virginia Military District** (metes-and-bounds survey, for Virginia Revolutionary War veterans) and the **Connecticut Western Reserve** (gridded survey, in northeastern Ohio), per the same Wiki page's Land Records section (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records).

## Boundary changes
- The Northwest Territory (1787) originally covered present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin and part of Minnesota.
- Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790) were the first two counties carved out — further county splits continued through the period, so **you must identify which county held jurisdiction over your ancestor's location at the specific date of the event**, not assume today's county boundaries apply.
- Ohio became a state, and a standalone jurisdiction, only in 1803 — records before that date are territorial, filed under the Northwest Territory or its organized counties, not under "Ohio" as a state.
- `place_search_all` returned no historical-jurisdiction chain for "Ohio" in this tool's data, so the territorial predecessor is not resolvable through that tool directly; the FamilySearch Wiki narrative above is the available source for the succession.

## Available record types

### Land records
- **Survey systems:** Virginia Military District used metes-and-bounds; the Connecticut Western Reserve used a rectangular/grid survey — different systems in different parts of the territory (FamilySearch Wiki, Ohio Genealogy#Land_Records).
- **Where held:** Virginia Military District warrants are held at the Virginia State Library; Connecticut Western Reserve records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.
- **Digitized:** `collections_search` lists "Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840" (collection 1542187, 234,567 people) — indexed on FamilySearch. `volume_search` also found a browse-only, 0%-indexed volume of **Territorial Land Records, 1788-1799** for the Northwest Territory (image group 005112233, 51 images, no name index, no full-text) — this must be browsed image by image.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- No statewide system existed in this period — Ohio wasn't a state until 1803. `collections_search` lists "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013" (collection 1803785, over 3 million people), which does reach back into this era at the county level.
- Births and deaths at this early date are not covered by any dedicated indexed collection found: the only online death collection returned ("Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001", collection 1417891) starts well after 1803 — a clear gap for the 1790 period.

### Church records
- `collections_search` lists "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (collection 2246917, 678,234 people) — this is the main substitute for missing early vital records and does cover the target window from its very start date.
- The FamilySearch Wiki generically confirms church registers often predate civil registration and are frequently the only vital-event source for early periods — check both denominational archives and FamilySearch microfilm.

### Census records
- The first federal census was taken in 1790, but the Northwest Territory was not enumerated as settled states were — no 1790 federal schedule exists for Ohio specifically. No territorial or state census for this exact window was returned by any tool here; this is a documented gap, not confirmed coverage.

### Tax records
- `collections_search` lists "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850" (collection 1987542, 345,890 people) — begins right at the edge of statehood, a useful substitute for the missing 1790s census.

### Military records
- No records specific to this 1788–1803 window were returned by any tool. The generic FamilySearch guidance notes service, pension, and bounty-land records are held at the National Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages 1789-2013 (1803785); Ohio, Tax Records 1800-1850 (1987542); Ohio, Church Records 1787-1950 (2246917); Ohio, Land Records 1787-1840 (1542187); Ohio, County Death Records 1840-2001 (1417891); Territorial Land Records 1788-1799 (image group 005112233, browse-only); Washington County Tax Records 1799-1803 (image group 005112240, partly indexed) | Church Records substitutes for missing early vital registration; Tax Records substitutes for the missing territorial census | Free |

## Records NOT online
Territorial-era probate, guardianship, and court records; original Virginia Military District warrant files; original Connecticut Western Reserve land records — all reported only as physical holdings above, with no online collection surfaced by this survey.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that any specific Ohio/Northwest Territory record series was destroyed. The absence of an 1790s census or an online probate/court collection is a coverage gap observed in this survey, not a confirmed loss — do not treat it as evidence the records never existed.

## Research tips
- Determine the exact county of jurisdiction (Washington from 1788, Hamilton from 1790, or others organized later) for the specific date of your ancestor's event, since Northwest Territory county boundaries changed repeatedly (FamilySearch Wiki, Ohio Genealogy#Northwest_Territory, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory).

- `catalog_search` returned no hits for Ohio — search the FamilySearch Catalog again later or consult the Ohio History Connection's own finding aids directly, since this survey could not confirm catalog holdings.

---
This covers the area that became Ohio during the years just before it was a state, roughly 1788 to 1803, when it was actually part of the larger "Northwest Territory" and divided into early counties like Washington and Hamilton rather than the Ohio we know today. Surviving records from this early, sparsely documented period are thin: there was no state and essentially no regular census, so the best substitutes are church registers (which exist from 1787), land records tied to two special land-grant zones (one for Virginia war veterans, one for Connecticut settlers, each kept at a different historical society), and early tax lists, while most court and estate records from that time survive only on paper at county courthouses or the Ohio History Connection in Columbus rather than online. # Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Statehood:** California became a state in 1850, bypassing territorial status.
- **Trigger event:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, Coloma, January 24, 1848; roughly 300,000 migrants arrived from the U.S. and abroad, producing a transient, predominantly male population.
- **Prior jurisdiction:** Spanish colonial territory, then Mexico — mission-era records (1769–1834) predate the Gold Rush and are background context, not primary sources for 1848–1860.

---

## Key Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **California, County Births, 1850–1919** (FamilySearch collection id 2017276, ~789,456 people) — begins at the start of the Gold Rush window.
- **California, County Marriages, 1850–1952** (FamilySearch collection id 1452832, ~1,135,780 people) — also starts in 1850.
- Both are held at the **county level**; search at [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org).
- ⚠️ A California-specific statewide vital-registration start date could **not be confirmed** in this survey — check the FamilySearch Wiki's dedicated California Vital Records page before assuming any date.

### Census Records
- **1850 Federal Census** — the first federal census taken in California, but some county returns are **known to be missing/destroyed**. The FamilySearch Wiki does not specify which counties, so treat any absence as a possible loss.
- **California State Census, 1850–1852** — a digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001, 522 images, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable) — can be searched by name on FamilySearch. Use this alongside the federal census to fill gaps.
- The **1852 California state census** is also named as a key Gold Rush source by the FamilySearch Wiki.

### Mining & Occupational Records
- **Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855** (imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images) — digitized but **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable: browse-only**. Must be paged through manually.
- Recorded at the county/district level.

### Immigration & Port Arrival Records
- **Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** (imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images) — also **browse-only, no name index**.
- **San Francisco ship passenger manifests**, held at **NARA's San Bruno facility**, are the main resource for those who arrived by sea.
- For overland migrants, the FamilySearch Wiki names **overland-trail diaries and journals** as a parallel source.

### Church Records
- **California, Mission Records, 1769–1850** (FamilySearch id 1804372, ~98,765 people) — overlaps only the very start of this period; primarily a pre-Gold Rush, Spanish/Mexican-era series.

### Great Registers (Voter Records)
- **California, Great Registers, 1866–1910** (FamilySearch id 1923340) — begin *after* this period but are useful for tracking a migrant's continued presence in California into the 1860s.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What It Covers | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch.org | County births, marriages, mission records, state census | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1850/1860 federal census | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (obituaries, mining-camp notices) | Subscription |
| National Archives (NARA) | Passenger manifests, land patents, naturalization | Free finding aids |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **National Archives, San Bruno, CA** | San Francisco ship passenger manifests |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections |
| **California State Library** | Gold Rush-era manuscripts, state records |
| **County courthouses** (mining counties) | Mining claim registers, deeds, probate |

---

## Records NOT Online (Browse-Only Images)
- Mining Claim Registers (San Francisco, 1849–1855) and Port Arrival Registers (Sacramento, 1849–1858) are digitized as images only — they **cannot be searched by name**. Finding an ancestor in them requires paging through images date by date, location by location.

## Known Record Losses
- Some 1850 federal census county returns for California are confirmed missing; the FamilySearch Wiki does not specify which counties. Verify on a county-by-county basis.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Use both censuses together** — search the 1850–1852 state census (88% indexed on FamilySearch) alongside the 1850 federal census to compensate for lost federal county returns.
2. **For sea arrivals**, search San Francisco passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno; for land arrivals, look for overland-trail diary/journal collections.
3. **Mining claim registers** require manual browsing — plan to narrow the search by date and location before paging through images.
4. **Bancroft Library and California State Library** hold Gold Rush manuscripts not digitized online — an in-person visit or written request may be needed.
5. **Great Registers start in 1866**, so they won't document arrival but can confirm continued California residence afterward.

---

## Recommended Next Step
Identify the **specific county** where your ancestor settled or mined — for example, El Dorado, Placer, Calaveras, or Sacramento — so that a county-level guide can be built around that courthouse's actual holdings. County-level vital, probate, court, and land records will give you much more targeted guidance than the state level alone.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (Colonial 1700s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
New York City originated as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam (1626), seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York. It served as capital of the British Province of New York through the 1700s. The jurisdiction falls under the Province of New York (British colonial administration) until 1783, then New York State from 1788.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(Primary vital-event source for this era)*
- **Denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest, beginning 1639), Anglican/Trinity Church, Presbyterian
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Online:** FamilySearch holds a digitized Dutch Reformed Church Registers volume (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 211 images, 1700–1776) — **browse-only, 0% indexed, written in Dutch (nl)**
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" (collection id 1469062, 2,345,678 people)
- ⚠️ No digitized Anglican/Trinity Church or Presbyterian registers were found for this period — seek those from the denominations' own archives

### Probate Records
- Wills proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York**; abstracts were published by the New-York Historical Society
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (collection id 1542780, 987,654 people)

### Land Records
- Colonial land conveyances and patents survive from this period
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (collection id 2078654, 1,567,890 people)

### Tax & Military Records *(Census substitutes — no federal census exists before 1790)*
- Tax assessment lists (ward-level) and militia rolls survive for some years
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (collection id 1678432) — covers only the very end of the colonial period

### Census Records
- **No federal census exists before 1790.** Use tax lists and militia rolls as substitutes for the 1700s.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records, land, probate, tax rolls, Dutch Reformed browse volumes | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1790+ only — does not cover colonial years) | Subscription |

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **New-York Historical Society** | Abstracts of Wills (Prerogative Court), colonial manuscripts |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** | Extensive colonial-era collections |
| **New York State Archives** | New York Colonial Manuscripts |

---

## Records NOT Online (Confirmed Gaps)
- Trinity Church (Anglican) and Presbyterian registers for the 1700s were **not found** as digitized collections — treat as held physically by the denominations unless confirmed otherwise
- Mayor's Court records and colonial court minute books were referenced in research sources but no digitized collection was found

1. **Dutch Reformed registers are the earliest continuous series** (1700–1776) but are unindexed and in Dutch — plan to browse page by page and read Dutch, or look for a published translation.
2. **Start with published will abstracts** before searching original Prerogative Court files — the New-York Historical Society abstracted these and they are more accessible.

New York City in the 1700s was a bustling colonial port city, and the records that survive from that era are mostly church registers rather than government birth/death certificates, since there was no statewide vital-records system yet; the Dutch Reformed Church kept the oldest and most complete registers, though the one digitized set found here is unindexed and written in Dutch, so it has to be browsed page by page. # Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies, operating as the independent Commonwealth of Virginia during the war years, organized by county. It contributed more troops to the American Revolution than any other colony/state, and major engagements (including the siege of Yorktown) were fought on Virginia soil.

---

## Available Record Types

### Military Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection id 1945678) — indexed + images. Build the link as: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678
- **Continental Line service records & muster rolls:** Held at the National Archives (Record Group 93)
- **Pension and bounty-land warrant applications:** NARA Record Group 15 — widows and heirs often filed decades later, naming the veteran's family
- **Virginia militia records:** Library of Virginia, Richmond
- **Bounty-warrant volume:** Image group 005301447 (341 images, browse-only, 1779–1800)

### Land Records (Bounty Lands)
- Virginia granted bounty lands in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** to its veterans; warrant and survey records are at the Virginia State Library
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection id 1734285)

### Tax Records — Key Substitute for Destroyed 1790 Census
- **⚠️ The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. County tax lists from the 1780s are the stated substitute.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection id 1456723) — indexed + images
- **Volume:** Image group 005301449 (87 images, full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed, 1782–1799) — search by typed name, not a name index

### Court Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection id 2134567)
- **Augusta County court order books:** Image group 005301448 (158 images, 61% name-indexed, 1775–1795) — a negative name-search here does not rule out a match; some images must still be browsed

### Church Records
- The Anglican/Episcopal church was the state church through the Revolution; parish vestry books recorded births, marriages, and burials
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection id 1598230)

### Civil Vital Registration
- Virginia's civil vital-registration start date could not be confirmed from the FamilySearch Wiki for this period. For 1775–1783, rely on parish/church records and court/land/tax records instead.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What It Covers | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Military, land, tax, court, church collections listed above | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Continental Line service (RG 93), pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free guidance; varied record access |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Census and supplementary records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records |
| Virginia State Library | Bounty-land warrant & survey records |
| County courthouses | Deed books, court order books, probate records |
| National Archives (NARA) | Continental Line muster rolls (RG 93); pension & bounty-land files (RG 15) |

---

## Research Tips
1. **Use 1780s tax lists as your 1790 census substitute** — the original 1790 Virginia federal census no longer exists.
2. **Check both state militia and Continental Line records** — a soldier could appear in one and not the other.
3. **Search pension files even for non-veterans** — widows and heirs filed on behalf of veterans, often naming the entire family.
4. **The Augusta County court order books are only 61% indexed** — a negative name search there is not conclusive; browse remaining images manually.
5. **The 1782–1799 tax-list volume is full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — search it by typing the name as a text query.

---
