# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; it did not become a state recognized in FamilySearch's place index until 1788 (`place_search` standardPlace dateRange "+1788/"), so during the war years 1775–1783 it operated as the independent Commonwealth of Virginia, still organized by county.
- **Key historical events:** Per Wikipedia, Virginia contributed more troops to the American Revolution than any other colony/state, and major engagements (including the siege of Yorktown) were fought on Virginia soil (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia).
- **Population during the period:** `place_population` returned no usable data for Virginia for 1775–1783 — this survey could not confirm population figures for the period.
- **Record-keeping depth:** Wikipedia notes Virginia kept county-level records from the 1630s, giving deep colonial-era documentation (parish registers, court order books, land patents, tax lists) that predates and overlaps the Revolution.

## Boundary changes
Virginia's county structure was already well established by 1775 and continued to subdivide during and after the war (new counties were regularly carved from older ones). This survey did not pull a county-by-county boundary list; if you have a specific ancestral county in mind, a follow-up guide at the county level (e.g., Augusta County, which appears below) would pin down exact boundary history for that locality.

## Available record types

### Military records
- **What exists:** FamilySearch's wiki search surfaced Continental Line service records and muster rolls held at the National Archives (Record Group 93), Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, and pension/bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15), plus published Virginia State Navy records (FamilySearch Wiki, "Virginia Military Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Where held:** A `collections_search` hit, "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection id 1945678, ~345,678 person count), covers exactly this period — build its link as https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678.
- **Digitized volumes:** `volume_search` found one volume of "Revolutionary War land bounty warrants" (image group 005301447, 341 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only, 1779–1800) covering Virginia statewide.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (the collection above) for general military records; browse-only images for the bounty-warrant volume.

### Land records (bounty lands)
- **What exists:** Veterans received bounty-land warrants; the FamilySearch Wiki notes Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans, with warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connecting veterans to their claims (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Where held:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection id 1734285, ~2,567,890 person count) spans this period; the dedicated bounty-warrant image volume (005301447, browse-only) above is the direct wartime/post-war record of the warrants themselves.
- **Access level:** Mixed — the general land/marriage/will collection is indexed; the bounty-warrant volume is browse-only images.

### Tax records
- **What exists:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes county tax lists from the 1780s are among the earliest substitutes for the 1790 Virginia federal census, which was destroyed (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Where held:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection id 1456723, ~456,789 person count). A `volume_search` hit also found a "State enumerations / tax lists" volume (image group 005301449, 87 images, 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable, 1782–1799) for Virginia statewide.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images for the main collection; full-text searchable but not name-indexed for the 1782–1799 volume — flag this explicitly, since it must be searched by text string, not by browsing a name index.

### Known record loss — census
- **1790 Virginia federal census:** Destroyed. The FamilySearch Wiki search result states the 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). Tax lists (see above) are the stated substitute for this loss.

### Court records
- **What exists:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection id 2134567, ~1,789,012 person count) spans the war years; county court order books recorded road and poor-relief business as well as suits and could name people with no military record at all.
- **Specific example found:** A `volume_search` hit for Augusta County, Virginia, found a county court order books volume (image group 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, 1775–1795) — this is a concrete, partially indexed starting point if your ancestors were in or near Augusta County.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images for the general collection; the Augusta County volume is partially indexed (61%), so a negative name search there does not rule out a match.

### Church records
- **What exists:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection id 1598230, ~1,234,567 person count) covers the war period; the established Anglican/Episcopal church was the state church through the Revolution, so parish vestry books often recorded births, marriages, and burials where no civil vital registration existed.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** This survey could not confirm a specific statewide civil-registration start date for Virginia from the FamilySearch Wiki — the Virginia-specific "Vital Records" page did not return jurisdiction-specific content (the fetch resolved to a generic "Genealogy Research Guide" page instead). For 1775–1783, treat parish/vestry church records and the court/land/tax records above as the primary sources, not civil vital registration.

### Immigration/emigration, cemetery, and newspaper records
- Not specifically surveyed for the wartime period by the tools above; `external_links_search` (see repository guide) surfaces general national resources (Find A Grave, Newspapers.com) that may hold incidental coverage, but no Virginia-specific 1775–1783 collections were returned for these record types.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (id 1945678); "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (id 1734285); "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (id 1456723); "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (id 2134567); "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (id 1598230) | Military service, bounty land, destroyed-1790-census substitute, courthouse business, parish vital events | Free |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | General military records | Military records gap noted above | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Continental Line service/pension/bounty-land files (RG 93, RG 15) per FamilySearch Wiki | Federal military and pension records | Free (research guidance); records access varies |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Post-war census (census destroyed for 1790 Virginia — see tax-list substitute) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Cemetery records gap (not separately surveyed) | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspapers | Newspaper records gap (not separately surveyed) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 3 digitized volumes total for Virginia in this period (bounty warrants, Augusta County court order books, and state tax lists) — this is the complete result set returned, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Virginia militia records, per FamilySearch Wiki | In-person / mail request |
| Virginia State Library | Bounty-land warrant and survey records connecting veterans to Virginia Military District (Ohio) claims, per FamilySearch Wiki | In-person / mail request |
| County courthouses | Original deed books, court order books, probate records | In-person / mail |
| National Archives (NARA) | Continental Line muster rolls (RG 93), pension and bounty-land application files (RG 15) | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online
This survey's `catalog_search` for "Revolutionary War" in Virginia returned zero hits (a cataloguing gap in the Catalog index, not evidence records don't exist). Treat the Library of Virginia's militia records and the Virginia State Library's warrant/survey records as likely physical-only or microfilm holdings unless and until a specific online collection is confirmed for them.

## Known record losses
The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed, per the FamilySearch Wiki result cited above (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The stated substitute is the county tax lists from the 1780s ("Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850," collection id 1456723, and the full-text-searchable 1782–1799 tax-list volume, image group 005301449).

## Research tips
- Because the 1790 census was destroyed, use the 1780s county tax lists as your head-of-household substitute for that era (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- Search pension and bounty-land warrant application files at NARA (RG 15) even for ancestors who are not confirmed veterans — widows and heirs often filed decades later, naming the veteran's family.
- If your ancestor served, check both state militia records (Library of Virginia) and Continental Line muster rolls (NARA RG 93) — a man could appear in one and not the other.
- The Augusta County court order books (image group 005301448) are only 61% name-indexed — a non-hit on a name search does not mean the record is absent; browse the remaining images.
- The 1782–1799 state tax-list volume (image group 005301449) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — search it by typing the name as a text query, not by browsing a name index.
- This survey could not confirm Virginia's civil vital-registration start date from the FamilySearch Wiki (the jurisdiction-specific page did not return specific content); rely on parish/vestry church records for births, marriages, and deaths in this period until that is confirmed.

I was not given a project to save this guide into, so it exists only in this reply — tell me if you'd like it persisted to a project, or want the same survey run at the county level for a specific ancestral county.

---

I looked into Virginia's genealogy records specifically for the Revolutionary War years, 1775 to 1783. Old military and government records survive well for this place and time: muster rolls and militia lists at the Library of Virginia and the National Archives, pension and land-bounty paperwork for veterans and their widows, county court order books, church (parish) registers, and tax lists that stand in for the 1790 census, which was destroyed in a later fire. The biggest warning is that the main national headcount for 1790 no longer exists, so tax lists from the 1780s are the best substitute for finding a family by name and location; another is that some of these old record books are digitized as plain images you must flip through page by page rather than search by typed name, so patience is needed even when a record is "online."

Next, if you can tell me the specific county or family surname you're tracing, I can build a more detailed, county-level version of this guide or help search these record sets directly.

---

## New Orleans, Louisiana — Record Survival After Disasters (Early 1800s)

### What Was Lost
- **Fires of 1788 and 1794** destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era documents.
- Later **floods, hurricanes, and yellow fever outbreaks** caused further archival damage.

### What Survived and Where to Look

| Record Type | Coverage | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **St. Louis Cathedral Catholic registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) | From 1731, with some gaps | Diocese archives / microfilm |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives** (notarial acts — deeds, successions, contracts) | From 1734; 30+ million pages | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center |
| **Spanish Cabildo government records** | Colonial period | Louisiana State Archives / Historic New Orleans Collection |
| **Probate / succession records** | Early 1800s | Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge |

### Key Points for Researchers

1. **Notarial acts are the primary substitute** for many record types that burned. Louisiana's French/Spanish legal tradition recorded nearly everything through a notary — property sales, wills, contracts, and family agreements — so these stand in for records lost elsewhere.

2. **Catholic sacramental registers** are the main substitute for vital records. Because Louisiana had no civil registration until 1853, church records are the only systematic record of births, marriages, and deaths for this period.

3. **Caution on the notarial microfilm**: The only digitized notarial volume covering 1803–1820 found in FamilySearch is **unindexed browse-only microfilm**, partly in French — it must be paged through image by image, not searched by name.

4. **Verify FamilySearch Wiki specifics directly**: Some detail pages returned generic boilerplate rather than New-Orleans-specific content, so dates and collection details should be confirmed on the FamilySearch Research Wiki itself.

---

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — 1840s Immigration Records

## Jurisdiction Overview
Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts was a major U.S. port of entry in the 1840s, especially for Irish immigrants fleeing the Famine (1845–1852). Wikipedia notes that by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born.

---

## Key Record Types for 1840s Immigrant Research

### 📋 Passenger / Immigration Lists
- **Customs Passenger Lists (1820–1891):** The primary source for Port of Boston arrivals. These are held originally at the **National Archives at Boston (Waltham)** as Record Group 36. They are indexed on **FamilySearch** ("Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891") and **Ancestry**.
- **Important caveat:** 1840s lists give only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — far less detail than post-1890s manifests.
- **Digitized volume:** One matching image group (003345210, 389 images) covers Boston 1840–1850, but it is only **3% name-indexed**. Use **full-text search** rather than relying on name-index lookup.

### ⛪ Church Records (Essential for Irish Catholic families)
- Catholic parishes such as the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the 1840s onward.
- Held at the **Archdiocese of Boston Archives**; also partially available on FamilySearch (collection: "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920").
- These records are **critical** when civil vital registration is absent or unclear.

### 📰 Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Town-level records predate statewide registration in Massachusetts. FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890."
- The exact statewide registration start date was **not confirmed** in this survey — verify before assuming a record exists.

### 🗺️ Census Records
- Federal census records for **1840** and **1850** cover this period and can help locate an immigrant family after arrival.

### ⚖️ Naturalization Records
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in almost *any* court of record. FamilySearch collection: "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (345,678 people indexed).

### 📰 Newspaper Notices
- **The Pilot** (Irish Catholic newspaper) published arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements for immigrants. No confirmed online digitization was found in this survey — check newspaper archive services like **Newspapers.com** or contact the Boston Public Library.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Passenger lists, vital records, church records, naturalization, probate | Free |
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham)** | Original Port of Boston customs passenger lists, RG 36 | In-person or written request |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | Contact directly |
| **Ancestry** | Census, passenger lists | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers (arrival/missing-persons notices) | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search full-text, not just the name index** — the digitized Boston passenger-list volume is barely name-indexed; full-text search is essential.
2. **Go to Catholic parish registers early** — for Irish families arriving in the 1840s, these often bridge gaps before civil registration was reliable.
3. **Don't stop at the passenger list** — once you locate an arrival, trace the family in the 1850 census, naturalization records, and Catholic registers to build out the picture.
4. **The Pilot newspaper** can be a surprising source for immigrant arrival and "seeking relatives" notices. The Boston Public Library may hold runs of this paper.
5. **Catalog caution:** The FamilySearch Catalog search returned no hits for Boston passenger lists in this survey — consult the Catalog directly or NARA's RG 36 finding aids for a full picture of what is held.

---

**Summary:** The core starting point is the Port of Boston customs passenger lists (available via FamilySearch and Ancestry), combined with Catholic parish registers from the Archdiocese of Boston for Irish families. Because the 1840s lists contain minimal information, supplement them with the 1850 federal census, naturalization court filings, and Irish Catholic newspaper notices to fully trace an immigrant ancestor's arrival and settlement.

output.text_response:
## Locality Guide: Native American Records in Oklahoma / Indian Territory (Mid-1800s)

---

### Jurisdiction Overview

Oklahoma did **not exist as a jurisdiction until statehood in 1907**. In the mid-1800s, the relevant jurisdiction was **Indian Territory** — land designated under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for relocated tribes, including the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) via the Trail of Trails. No county seat or standard civil administrative center existed; authority ran through federal Indian agencies and tribal governments.

> **Tip:** Always search under both "Indian Territory" *and* "Oklahoma" as place names — FamilySearch's collections span both labels in a single continuous set.

---

### Key Record Types

#### 1. Tribal Rolls and Enrollment Records
The most essential source for this period.

- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** and **Drennen Roll (1852)** are the key mid-1800s rolls (per FamilySearch Wiki's "Oklahoma Native American Records" page).
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** are the most widely used enrollment records for the Five Civilized Tribes, though they fall later than your target period.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (collection id 1987432, ~567,890 people)
- **Digitized Volume:** Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870 (image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable) — reachable via FamilySearch record search or full-text search.

#### 2. Land Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (collection id 1541872, ~234,567 people) — directly covers the mid-1800s target period.

#### 3. Church / Mission Records
Christian missionaries (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) worked among relocated tribes from the 1820s onward, keeping registers of converts, students, and community members.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (id 1654321, ~123,456 people) — overlaps the mid-1800s target period.

#### 4. Federal / Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records
The BIA kept annuity payment rolls, correspondence, and school records — now held at the **National Archives (NARA)**. These fill in names and events not captured in tribal rolls.

#### 5. Treaty Records
Ratified Indian treaties from the 1830s–1860s are federal records held at NARA. No specific online collection was confirmed by this survey — treat as a research gap requiring direct NARA inquiry.

#### 6. Vital Records (Civil Registration)
**Civil birth, marriage, and death registration did not exist in Indian Territory in the mid-1800s** — there was no state or territorial government to administer it. The closest FamilySearch vital-type collection, *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* (id 2134789), only starts in 1890, after county courts existed.

#### 7. Tribal Court and Probate Records
Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained their own court systems. No specific online collection was confirmed in this survey — a gap worth pursuing directly with NARA or the specific tribal nation's own archives.

---

### Repository Guide

| Repository | Collections / Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (id 1987432); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (id 1541872); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (id 1654321); Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870 (image group 002298871) | Free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | BIA agency records, annuity rolls, treaty files, allotment case files | In-person or online request |
| **Tribal Nation Archives** | Tribal court records, probate records, tribal government records | Contact each nation directly |

---

### Research Tips

1. **Identify the tribal nation first.** Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole each kept separate rolls and have their own NARA record groups. This one step determines where to look first.

2. **Start with the mid-1800s rolls** — the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) are the most targeted starting points for your period. The Tribal Enrollment Cards digitized volume (1840–1870) is searchable by name on FamilySearch.

3. **Check BIA agency records at NARA** for annuity payment rolls, school records, and correspondence that fill in family members not found on the rolls themselves.

4. **Check missionary registers** (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) for baptisms, school enrollments, and congregation lists that predate any civil registration.

5. **Search under both place names** — "Indian Territory" for mid-1800s records, and "Oklahoma" for later ones. FamilySearch treats them as one continuous research trail in many collections.

6. **For detailed tribal-specific guidance**, run targeted FamilySearch Wiki searches for terms like "Dawes Commission," "Cherokee Nation records," or the specific tribe you're researching.

---

**Next step:** Identify which tribal nation your family belonged to — that is the single most important step before searching, as it determines which rolls, record groups, and repositories to prioritize.

subagents.description: Locality guide for Pennsylvania Quaker records

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide produced for Pennsylvania Quaker communities in the late 1700s:

---

## Locality Guide: Quaker Communities in Pennsylvania, 1750–1800

### The Records Landscape

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths in this period — the first such laws came much later. This means **Quaker meeting records are the primary substitute** for vital records for families in this community.

### What Meeting Records Contain

Monthly meeting minute books routinely recorded:
- **Births** of members' children
- **Marriages** (with approval process documented)
- **Deaths and burials**
- **Certificates of removal** (transfers between meetings when families moved)
- **Disownments and disciplinary cases** (which often name family members)

These records can be extraordinarily detailed and consistent compared to civil or church records of the same era.

### Key Finding Aid

**Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** — a six-volume published abstract of meeting records — is the standard starting point. It indexes names from many Pennsylvania monthly meetings and is widely available in genealogical libraries and on microfilm.

### Where the Original Records Are Held

Most monthly-meeting-level minute books for the heavily Quaker counties — **Chester, Bucks, and Delaware** — are held at two repositories:

1. **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA)
   - The primary repository for Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records and many constituent monthly meetings.
2. **Quaker Collection, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA)
   - Holds additional meeting records and related manuscript collections.

Both repositories should be contacted directly; most of the minute books at this level have **not been digitized** and require on-site or correspondence research.

### Digitized Resource (with Limitations)

A digitized set of **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes** covering this period was located online, but it has **no name index** — it must be browsed page by page. Yearly meeting minutes record broader governance but refer to specific cases handled at the monthly-meeting level, so they are most useful for context rather than as a primary name search.

### Important Caution: Meeting Boundaries ≠ County Lines

Quaker meeting boundaries did **not align neatly with county lines**. A family should be searched by **meeting name** as well as by county. If you know the township where the family lived, tracing which monthly meeting covered that township is essential before searching the minutes.

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Search Hinshaw's** for the family surname to identify which monthly meeting(s) recorded them.
2. **Contact Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore** or **Haverford's Quaker Collection** to request access to or copies from the relevant minute books.
3. Use **certificates of removal** to trace migration — if a family moved from, say, Chester County to a western Pennsylvania meeting, there will be a removal certificate filed at both the sending and receiving meetings.
4. Ask a **research-plan** to be built for the specific ancestors once the meeting is identified.

# Locality Guide: Quaker (Religious Society of Friends) communities in Pennsylvania (1750-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania became a state in 1787; founded as a colony by William Penn in 1682 as a haven for Quakers (per Wikipedia, "Quakers in Pennsylvania").
- **County seat / administrative center:** N/A at state level; densest Quaker settlement in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties (per Wikipedia).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States.
- **Population during period:** Not confirmed by this survey — `place_population` returned no data for Pennsylvania, United States for 1750-1800.
- **Economy:** Agricultural and mercantile communities organized around Quaker meetings in the counties named above.
- **Ethnic composition:** English and Welsh Quaker settlers predominated in the named counties by the late 1700s (per Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) organized in monthly, quarterly, and yearly meetings (per Wikipedia and the FamilySearch Wiki "Pennsylvania Church Records" page).
- **Key historical events:** Not confirmed by this survey for this specific period; see historical-context for deeper treatment.

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's own boundaries were largely settled by the 1780s; this survey did not confirm any boundary change affecting Quaker-meeting territory within 1750-1800.
- Quaker meeting boundaries (monthly/quarterly meeting catchments) did not track civil county lines exactly — a family's meeting of record may differ from its county of residence. Search by meeting name, not just by county.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania-specific vital-records page did not return jurisdiction-specific content in this survey (it fell back to a generic "Genealogy Records" page); per the wiki_search result on "Pennsylvania Church Records," statewide civil registration was not mandated until 1906.
- **What exists:** For 1750-1800, no statewide civil vital registration existed — Quaker meeting records fill this role for Quaker families.
- **Where held:** N/A for this period at the civil level.
- **Gaps:** Entire 1750-1800 window has no civil vital registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting minutes (births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal); see Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Religious Society of Friends (Quakers), organized by monthly meeting, with monthly meetings grouped into quarterly and yearly meetings (per Wikipedia, "Quakers in Pennsylvania," and the FamilySearch Wiki search result "Pennsylvania Church Records").
- **Record types:** Minutes of monthly, quarterly, and yearly meetings record births, marriages (with certificates signed by all attendees), deaths, certificates of removal (transfers between meetings), and disciplinary proceedings (disownments) — per the FamilySearch Wiki search result on "Pennsylvania Church Records."
- **Where held:** A digitized, browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750-1800, image group number 001188322, 145 images, covering Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was found via volume_search. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College and the Quaker and Special Collections at Haverford College are named as the primary repositories for original Quaker records (per Wikipedia).
- **Gaps:** This survey found only one digitized volume (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting) for 1750-1800; monthly-meeting-level minute books for Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties were not found in `volume_search` or `catalog_search` (catalog_search returned 0 hits for "Quaker Friends meeting records" in Pennsylvania) — a cataloguing/digitization gap, not evidence the records do not exist.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census begins 1790 for the United States; no 1750-1790 federal enumeration exists.
- **State/provincial census:** This survey did not confirm any Pennsylvania state census for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Not confirmed by this survey; tax lists (see Tax records) are the standard substitute for the pre-1790 years.
- **Access:** Not applicable for most of this period given no national enumeration before 1790.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, and inventories; `collections_search` returned "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection id 1999196), which overlaps the full 1750-1800 period.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not determinable without a named individual; check both will and administration series.
- **Date range:** 1683-1994 (per collection 1999196), so the full target period is covered.
- **Where held:** Collection 1999196 is held via FamilySearch; its personCount is 0 in the returned data, suggesting it is an unindexed or image-only collection — confirm at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not confirmed by this survey — the `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` wiki page was not fetched in this pass.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents; not itemized by this survey's tool results.
- **Date range:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by this survey; typically county recorder of deeds offices and the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The French and Indian War (1754-1763) and the American Revolutionary War (1775-1783) fall within this period, though Quakers generally practiced pacifism and are less likely to appear in service records (consistent with Quaker testimony per Wikipedia).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files; Quaker disownment records in meeting minutes sometimes note members disowned for military participation — a cross-reference worth checking in the meeting minutes above.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), per the generic FamilySearch Wiki fallback page read in this survey.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Quaker meetinghouses typically maintained their own burial grounds adjoining the meetinghouse; none named specifically by this survey's tool results.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave was returned by `external_links_search` as a curated resource (https://www.findagrave.com/).
- **Physical records:** Burial records were often kept within the meeting minutes themselves rather than as a separate sexton register (per the general pattern described in the FamilySearch Wiki search result on Pennsylvania Church Records).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Not confirmed by this survey for the 1750-1800 period.
- **Where held:** `external_links_search` returned Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) as a curated general resource for Pennsylvania.
- **Content value:** Limited for Quaker vital events in this period, since meeting minutes, not newspapers, were the primary record of births/marriages/deaths.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the principal port of entry for Quaker immigrants to Pennsylvania in the colonial period.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for the colonial period are sparse compared to the 19th century; certificates of removal in meeting minutes document a family's transfer from a Quaker meeting in Britain or Ireland to a Pennsylvania meeting, serving as a migration record.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by this survey beyond the general NARA reference from the FamilySearch Wiki fallback page.
- **Content note:** Review full family groups in any certificate of removal — these list every family member transferring together, including children.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Not itemized by this survey's tool results.
- **Date range:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by this survey; typically county level.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the standard substitute for the missing pre-1790 census in this period.

### Other record types
- William Wade Hinshaw's "Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy" (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states and is a key published finding aid (per the wiki_search result on "Pennsylvania Church Records").
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers beyond the single digitized volume found in this survey's volume_search (per the same wiki_search result).

---

## Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, PA — Late 1800s Steel Boom

### Civil Registration & Vital Records
- **Births, Deaths & Marriages** were recorded at the **county courthouse** well before Pennsylvania's statewide system. FamilySearch online collections pick up marriages from ~1885 and deaths from ~1906 onward; earlier originals require a courthouse visit or direct request.
- The **1880 and 1900 federal censuses** are especially valuable — both record each resident's occupation, and the 1900 census adds immigration year (critical for the immigrant mill workforce).

### Ethnic Church Records
Pittsburgh's steel mills drew massive waves of immigrants. Each community's parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) are held by the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives**:
- Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish parishes all kept their own records

### Occupational & Industrial Sources
No confirmed online collections were found for company-level records. Direct repositories to pursue:
- **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) — company payrolls, mill accident/compensation records, union rolls
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** — city directories dating back to 1813 (useful for tracking workers year to year)
- **National Archives at Philadelphia** — naturalization records for immigrant mill workers

### Next Steps
Hand this guide to **research-plan** to stage actual searches against these record types and repositories, and prioritize based on your specific ancestor's ethnicity, mill employer, or decade of arrival.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level recording of births and deaths from 1870; marriage licenses from 1885 at the county courthouse (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy wiki page) — earlier than Pennsylvania's 1906 statewide mandate.
- **What exists:** Births and deaths 1870 onward; marriage licenses 1885 onward, at the Allegheny County courthouse.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (originals); FamilySearch's "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 people) and "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" (collection 1921317, 1,048,378 people) cover the statewide-era portion online.
- **Gaps:** Statewide death certificates online only from 1906 — 1870-1905 Allegheny County deaths are not in that collection; check the county-level originals instead.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Ethnic Catholic parish baptism/marriage/burial registers from the 1840s onward (see Church records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Ethnic Catholic parishes — Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish — from the 1840s onward (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy wiki page).
- **Record types:** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers.
- **Where held:** The Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds many originals.
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm coverage or survival for individual parishes or specific years — check the diocesan archives directly.
- **Language:** Not stated by the tools used in this survey; given the ethnic parish makeup, expect registers possibly in Latin or the parish's ethnic language in addition to English — unconfirmed here.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census records for Allegheny County survive from 1800; the 1880 and 1900 censuses are particularly valuable for industrial workers, recording occupation, parents' birthplace, and (1900) immigration year (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy wiki page).
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Access:** volume_search (at the Pennsylvania level) did not return a dedicated census volume for this window; use Ancestry's U.S. Federal Census Collection (link below) or FamilySearch's standard census search.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories — "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196, personCount 0 — an unindexed/browse set) and the matching browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Testate or intestate:** Not known in advance — search both wills and administration series.
- **Date range:** 1683-1994 for the statewide probate collection; county court records likely run from the county's 1788 formation.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (originals); FamilySearch holds a browse-only digitized volume for the state series.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed — no `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` page was fetched in this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records — per the generic FamilySearch guidance retrieved, held at county courthouses.
- **Date range:** Not confirmed.
- **Where held:** County recorder of deeds (physical); not confirmed online in this survey.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** None specific to 1870-1900 were identified (post-Civil War, pre-Spanish-American War mobilization in this county); not confirmed by this survey.
- **Record types:** Service, pension, and draft records generally held at NARA per the FamilySearch generic guidance retrieved.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration; see Fold3 link below.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not confirmed by this survey for specific Pittsburgh-area cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (external link below).
- **Physical records:** Sexton/burial registers — not confirmed, likely held by individual cemeteries or parishes.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (external link below) for digitized coverage; local historical societies and libraries for physical runs.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and legal/mill-accident notices are a likely source for industrial-era workers, though no specific Pittsburgh paper was confirmed here.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Pittsburgh is inland; immigrants reaching it typically arrived via East Coast ports (not confirmed by this survey) before traveling inland.
- **Record types:** Naturalization petitions from the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas (1798-1930), held at the National Archives at Philadelphia (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy wiki page). FamilySearch also holds "Pennsylvania, Naturalization Records, 1790-1915" as a digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 351 images, 15% indexed, languages English and German, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** National Archives at Philadelphia; FamilySearch (partially indexed).
- **Content note:** Where passenger manifests are located for a family, review the full manifest — children and infants traveling with parents are listed alongside adults.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Date range:** Not confirmed.
- **Where held:** County courthouse, per generic FamilySearch guidance.
- **Substitute value:** Could substitute for missing vital-record years if located, but not confirmed here.

### Other record types
- **Occupational/industrial records:** No dedicated company, mill-payroll, or union-membership collection was returned by collections_search, volume_search, or catalog_search for Allegheny County in this survey (catalog_search returned 0 hits). Wikipedia's Pittsburgh summary names company records, union membership lists, and the Heinz History Center's industrial/immigration holdings as likely sources, but none of these were independently confirmed by a records tool in this run — treat as leads to verify directly with the Heinz History Center and the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (city directories from 1813, per the Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy wiki page), not as confirmed online collections.

Here is the locality guide the research agent compiled for **Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic**:

---

## Key Finding: Civil Registration Did Not Exist Yet

Pennsylvania had no statewide system for registering births, marriages, or deaths in 1793, so the most useful sources are not civil government records. Researchers instead rely on:

---

## Primary Record Types & Repositories

### 1. Church Burial Registers
The epidemic killed roughly 5,000 people (about 10% of Philadelphia's population), and churches recorded the burials. The most important registers are:
- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) — one of the largest congregations in the city
- **Gloria Dei ("Old Swedes'" Church)** — one of the oldest churches in Pennsylvania
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes** (Quakers) — a digitized but *unindexed* volume exists for 1750–1800; it must be browsed page by page, not searched by name

**Holdings:** Individual churches hold their own registers; some have been microfilmed or deposited at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**.

---

### 2. Contemporary Published Death List — Mathew Carey
Mathew Carey, a Philadelphia printer and civic figure, compiled and published a list of those who died in the epidemic. This is an invaluable name source for 1793 specifically.

**Holdings:** Held at **HSP** and in rare-book collections; some editions have been digitized.

---

### 3. Citizens' Relief Committee Records
Mayor Matthew Clarkson organized a citizens' committee to provide relief to the sick and to families of the dead. Their minutes and reports name individuals aided.

**Holdings:** **Philadelphia City Archives** and **HSP manuscript collections**.

---

### 4. Bush Hill Hospital Records
Bush Hill was the emergency fever hospital set up outside the city limits for epidemic victims. Records from this institution (admission lists, death records) document the sick and dying.

**Holdings:** **HSP manuscript collections**.

---

## Repositories to Contact

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Church registers (some), Carey's list, committee minutes, Bush Hill records, manuscript collections |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Municipal records, relief committee documents |
| **Individual churches** | Original burial registers |

---

## Important Caveats

1. **None of these turned up as searchable online FamilySearch collections** — they generally require a direct inquiry or an in-person/mail visit to HSP or the City Archives.
2. The FamilySearch Wiki's detailed pages for Philadelphia could not be fully retrieved during this search, so some specifics (exact church record date ranges, naturalization-court detail) should be verified directly with the repositories.
3. If the family was **Quaker**, the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting digitized volume (1750–1800) exists on FamilySearch but is unindexed — it would need to be browsed page by page.

---

## Suggested Next Step

A research plan can be built from this guide to sequence the actual searches, starting with the church burial registers and HSP's manuscript holdings. If you'd like me to build that plan, let me know the person or family you're tracing.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States (1793)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **City:** Philadelphia, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania (standardPlace "Philadelphia, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States", in existence since 1682 per place_search)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (also the Philadelphia County seat)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States; in 1793 Philadelphia was also the national capital
- **Population during period:** Wikipedia's summary of the 1793 epidemic states the city had roughly 50,000 residents and the fever killed about 5,000 — roughly one in ten — between August and November 1793 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). place_population returned no data for Philadelphia for this period, so these figures could not be cross-checked against FamilySearch's own population data this run.
- **Key historical events:** The yellow fever epidemic of August–November 1793, during which thousands fled the city and Mayor Matthew Clarkson's citizens' Committee organized relief and burials; physician Benjamin Rush left detailed accounts (Wikipedia, as above).

## Boundary changes
Philadelphia (city and county) has existed since 1682 per place_search, with no boundary change noted for the 1793 period by the tools in this survey (the city and county did not consolidate until 1854, outside this period). No further change affecting 1793 records was identified.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration of births, marriages or deaths in 1793; the FamilySearch Wiki's general record-types overview notes many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s, with no Philadelphia-specific start date confirmed this run.
- **What exists:** No civil vital registers for 1793 — church registers are the substitute (see Church records below).
- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period; see Church records.

### Church records
- **Denominations/congregations named for 1793 Philadelphia:** Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') are named by the FamilySearch Wiki's Philadelphia_Genealogy page as holding relevant burial records; a direct wiki_read of that page this run returned only generic fallback content, so denomination founding dates could not be independently confirmed.

# Locality Guide: Chicago (Cook County), Illinois — Great Fire of 1871

## Jurisdiction Overview
Cook County is the parent jurisdiction for Chicago. The **Great Chicago Fire** (October 8–10, 1871) killed roughly 300 people, destroyed ~3.3 square miles of the city, left over 100,000 homeless, and — critically for genealogists — **burned the Cook County Courthouse**, which housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
FamilySearch holds three key Cook County collections — all beginning in 1871 (immediately after the fire), consistent with the courthouse loss:
- **Birth Certificates, 1871–1940** (collection id 2024189)
- **Death Records, 1871–1947** (collection id 1913456)
- **Marriage Records, 1871–1920** (collection id 1756321)

> ⚠️ No FamilySearch collection for Cook County births/marriages/deaths **before 1871** was found — this is a direct consequence of the courthouse fire. Church registers are the primary substitute.

### Church Records
- FamilySearch: **"Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925"** (collection id 1803978) — spans both before and after the fire; a critical substitute for pre-fire baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- The **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers.

### Census Records
- **1870 federal census for Chicago survived** because original schedules were already filed in Washington, D.C. — this is your most important pre-fire household snapshot.
- 1850 and 1860 federal schedules are also available.

### Court & Probate Records
- A digitized FamilySearch volume: **"Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies)"**, 1865–1871 (image group 009982110) — browse-only, no name index.

### Land / Property Records
- The **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required Chicago property owners to re-register destroyed deeds. FamilySearch holds a digitized volume: **"Post-fire Property Re-recordings," 1871–1880** (image group 009982111) — 112 images, 41% name-indexed.
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company** insurance/property records at the **Chicago History Museum** are a vital substitute for pre-fire property ownership.

### City Directories
- Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward **survived the fire** and are held at the **Newberry Library** — valuable for locating families between census years and confirming pre/post-fire residence.

### Other Record Types
- **Newspapers:** Newspapers.com is listed for this place (fire coverage, casualty/property notices).
- **Military records:** Fold3 is listed among curated external links for Illinois/Cook County.
- **Cemetery records:** Find A Grave is listed for this place.
- **Immigration/naturalization:** NARA (archives.gov) for federal records.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Vital records 1871+, Church Records 1833–1925, reconstructed/re-recorded volumes | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1850/1860/1870 federal census | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Chicago newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military/pension records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Census, naturalization, land patents | Free |

### Physical / In-Person
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance/property records, photographs, personal papers |
| **Newberry Library** | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago, Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (NEIU)** | Cook County records post-1871 |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward |

---

## Known Record Losses
The fire destroyed the original Cook County deeds, birth/death registers, court records, and tax rolls. These are **gone**; only substitute or reconstructed records remain. The **Burnt Record Act re-recordings** and **insurance records** are the primary substitutes for property documentation.

---

## Research Strategy Summary

Because original courthouse records burned, build the family's pre-fire picture from **substitutes**:

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — it survived (originals were in Washington). Get the full household composition before the fire.
2. **Search Chicago city directories** at the Newberry Library to confirm residence and occupation just before/after the fire.
3. **Check FamilySearch's Church Records 1833–1925** for baptisms, marriages, and burials that predate civil registration.
4. **For property:** Search the Post-fire Property Re-recordings volume on FamilySearch (1871–1880, partly indexed), then contact the Chicago History Museum for the Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records.
5. **Post-fire vital records** (births, deaths, marriages from 1871 onward) are available on FamilySearch.

> **Note:** Several FamilySearch Wiki pages checked during this survey returned only generic content rather than place-specific detail. Treat exact record start dates and coverage notes as still needing direct verification on the FamilySearch Wiki. The FamilySearch Catalog also returned zero hits for Cook County in this survey — that reflects a cataloguing gap, not an absence of records; search the Catalog directly by title or keyword for further finds.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide for French colonial Louisiana (1700s), compiled by researching available sources and tools:

---

# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (approx. 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- France claimed Louisiana from 1682 and colonized it formally from 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville.
- Control shifted: French (1682–1762) → Spanish (Treaty of Fontainebleau, 1762) → briefly back to France, then sold to the U.S. in the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
- The Catholic Church was the sole legally recognized church. The *Code Noir* required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons.
- Colonial administration ran through the **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)**.

---

## Key Record Types

### 1. Catholic Church (Sacramental) Registers — *Primary Source*
- **What:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials — the closest equivalent to vital records in this era.
- **Oldest records:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans, holds registers from **1720**.
- **On FamilySearch:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection id 1612905, ~987,000 entries). Also digitized sacramental registers for the Archdiocese of New Orleans (image group 004330991, 264 images, 1720–1803) — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, written in French and Spanish**.
- **Physical repository:** Archdiocese of New Orleans (originals).

### 2. Colonial Administrative / Notarial Records
- **What:** Land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories, wills, marriage settlements — created by the Superior Council.
- **On FamilySearch:** Digitized image volume: "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)" covering Louisiana, 1699–1769, 149 images (image group 004330992) — **browse-only, 0% indexed, in French/Spanish**.
- **Physical repositories:**
  - **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) — partial digitization; in-person/archive request required for the rest.
  - **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — administrative correspondence and colonial census rolls; in-person or written request.

### 3. Land Records
- French concessions and later Spanish land grants (not U.S. rectangular-survey deeds).
- Documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series and at the **Louisiana State Land Office**.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the **1730s** onward — one of the oldest continuous notarial offices in North America.

### 4. Probate Records
- FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (id 2078341, ~456,000 entries) — starts mid-colonial/early-Spanish period, useful for the later part of the 1700s.

### 5. Colonial Census / Enumerations
- No federal census existed (U.S. federal enumeration begins 1790). Colonial-era population counts, where they survive, are in the ANOM administrative correspondence/census rolls in France.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church records, probate, digitized Superior Council and sacramental-register image sets | Free |
| Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans) | Superior Council records (land grants, court, contracts, estates) | In-person / archive request |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Contracts, wills, marriage settlements, 1730s onward | In-person / public access |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans | Original sacramental registers from 1720 | Archive request |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative correspondence, colonial census rolls | In-person / written request |
| Louisiana State Land Office | French/Spanish-era land grant records | In-person / written request |

---

## Practical Tips

1. **Language:** The two key digitized FamilySearch volumes (sacramental registers and Superior Council notarial acts) are in **French** and sometimes **Spanish**, not indexed by name. You must browse image by image.
2. **Start with Catholic registers:** The Church was the sole legal institution recording baptisms, marriages, and burials. The Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers (from 1720) are your first stop.
3. **For property, wills, and contracts:** Go to the Superior Council notarial acts and the New Orleans Notarial Archives — not U.S.-style deed books.
4. **For colonial census material:** Contact ANOM in France, as surviving population enumerations are in their overseas colonial archives, not on major genealogy platforms.
5. **Later collections don't cover this era:** Collections like "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" and "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" begin well after the French colonial period.

---

The best path forward is to browse the FamilySearch digitized sacramental registers and Superior Council notarial acts for your family names, then request access to the Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM for deeper colonial-era research. If you'd like a focused research plan built around specific ancestors or questions, that's the natural next step.

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records: land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories | In-person/archive request |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Administrative correspondence, colonial census rolls | In-person/written request |

Original Superior Council land-grant/court/contract records at the Louisiana Historical Center, the ANOM administrative correspondence and census rolls in France, and most New Orleans notarial archive material from the 1730s onward are described by the FamilySearch Wiki search result as held physically, with only partial digitization — treat these as requiring an archive visit or written request rather than assuming full online access.

---
This covers Louisiana during the French colonial period, roughly the 1700s to 1803, when the territory passed from France to Spain and then to the United States. The best surviving records from that era are Catholic Church registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials (since the Catholic Church was the only legal religion and the main record-keeper of the period), along with colonial government and notarial records covering land grants, contracts, wills, and estate matters, mostly held in New Orleans archives and in France's overseas colonial archive. Several of these are digitized by FamilySearch but only as browsable image sets, not searchable by name, and they are written in French and sometimes Spanish, so you will need to read the original documents page by page rather than search by name; some of the most important original material still exists only on paper in archives in New Orleans and France, requiring an in-person visit or written request.

The next step would be to have a research plan built around these specific record sets, or to start requesting access to the New Orleans and France-based archives for the family names you're tracing.

---

**Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1870–1900)**

**Key Context**

Pennsylvania had **no statewide vital registration** (births and deaths) until 1906, so there is no central state registry to consult for this era. The main substitute record types are:

- **Church registers** — baptism, marriage, and burial records filed at individual parishes (many churches in coal towns served Polish, Welsh, Irish, Slovak, and other immigrant mining communities)
- **County marriage licenses** — always filed at the county courthouse, not the state
- **Probate files** — at the county courthouse
- **County tax and land records**

**Notable Find: Mine-Worker Employment Cards**
A set of digitized, **name-searchable mine-worker employment cards** covers Schuylkill County miners for this exact period. This is a significant resource for identifying and tracing individual miners.

**Neighboring Counties to Check**
Mining companies operated across county lines, so families should check all three anthracite counties:
- **Schuylkill County** (employment cards, name-searchable)
- **Luzerne County** (mine-accident and payroll ledgers — browse only, no name search)
- **Lackawanna County** (similar to Luzerne — browse only)

**Repositories**
- County courthouses for marriage, probate, and land records
- Local churches for baptism, marriage, and burial registers — many require in-person or mailed requests; not all are online
- FamilySearch digitized collections for the searchable mine records

**Recommended Next Step**
Build a research plan beginning with the mine-worker employment cards and county marriage/probate indexes for the target families. If you'd like a plan created, just ask.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births and deaths did not begin until 1906 (FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)). Before that, a 1906-1968 death-certificate collection (FS collection 2255317, 4,218,763 people) only reaches into the tail end of the target period.
- **What exists:** Marriage licenses/bonds were kept at the county level from the colonial period — collection 1921317 "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" (1,048,378 people) and collection 1571957 "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (624,090 people) both cover 1870-1900.
- **Where held:** County courthouse (Schuylkill County Register of Wills/Clerk of Courts) for original marriage licenses; FamilySearch for the above indexed collections.
- **Gaps:** No births or deaths are civilly registered for Schuylkill County for 1870-1900 under this survey's findings — only marriages are covered at the county level.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (see Church records) and family Bibles.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not itemized by this survey's tool results for Schuylkill County specifically.
- **Record types:** A FamilySearch collection titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 982,415 people, 1708-1985) spans the target period and covers baptisms/marriages/burials generically.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (above collection); parish/denominational archives for originals — not named by this survey.
- **Gaps:** This survey could not confirm which denominations or years are missing from the collection above; re-check the FamilySearch Wiki or the collection's own description page.
- **Language:** Not stated by any tool result in this survey; given the immigrant population (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, German), expect some registers in languages other than English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Not confirmed as a named collection by this survey's `collections_search`, which returned marriage, death, and probate collections only, no census rows — this is a coverage gap in the results returned, not evidence the 1870/1880/1900 federal censuses are unavailable.
- **State/provincial census:** Not found in this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** None identified by this survey.
- **Access:** Not determined here — follow up with a dedicated `collections_search` pass scoped to census records.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not known in advance for a given ancestor — search both the will index and the administration index at the Register of Wills.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" spans the target period, though its `personCount` returned as 0 in this survey (an indexing gap, not proof of no records).
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills/Orphans' Court.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not detailed for Schuylkill County by this survey's results.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed — no `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` page was fetched in this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records (expected, not itemized here).
- **Date range:** Not determined by this survey.
- **Where held:** County Recorder of Deeds, by typical Pennsylvania practice — not specifically confirmed here.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Civil War service (1861-1865) is background for men who later worked the mines in 1870-1900; no specific conflict falls inside 1870-1900 itself.
- **Record types:** Service records, pensions, draft registrations — held at the National Archives per the generic FamilySearch guidance retrieved.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA); Fold3 is a curated external link returned for this place.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a curated external link returned for this place.
- **Physical records:** Sexton/burial registers — likely held by individual cemeteries or parishes; not itemized here.

### Newspaper records

- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a curated external link returned for this place.
- **Content value:** Mine-disaster reporting (e.g., the 1869 Avondale disaster) and obituaries are likely of high value in this coal-mining region, per the historical background above.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Not named here; anthracite-region immigrants typically arrived via Philadelphia or New York, per general background, not confirmed by a tool result in this survey.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists and naturalization petitions, including pre-1906 naturalizations that could be filed in any court of record (generic FamilySearch guidance retrieved in this survey).

Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691) were **separate jurisdictions** during this period and were not merged into a single Massachusetts province until 1691/1692. ---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording mandated beginning **1639**.

### Church Records
- **Denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) churches, the established church of the colony.
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings (admonishments, excommunications).
- **Digitization:** One full-text-searchable but unindexed volume found — image group 007612045, "Congregational church admissions and baptisms," covering Suffolk County, Massachusetts, 1630–1700, 121 images. FamilySearch also has "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection id 1921657, ~987,654 people).
- **Language:** English.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory — 1889 Land Run Era (1889–1907)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- The Land Run of April 22, 1889 opened the "Unassigned Lands" to settlement; Oklahoma Territory was formally organized in 1890. Oklahoma statehood did not occur until **1907**, when Oklahoma Territory merged with Indian Territory.
- Records for 1889–1907 should be sought under "Oklahoma Territory," not a modern county alone — many counties were not yet organized at the time of the run.

---

## Key Record Types & Repositories

### 🏞️ Land Records (highest priority)
- **General Land Office (GLO) homestead files** — Federal jurisdiction (Record Group 49), held at the **National Archives in Washington, D.C.** These are the richest source: application files, proof-of-settlement affidavits (naming witnesses/neighbors), final certificates, and patents.
- **BLM GLO Records site** (glorecords.blm.gov) — Free online index to homestead patents and certificates.
- **FamilySearch** — "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (74% name-indexed, also browsable as digitized images).
- ⚠️ Rejected homestead applications also survive and can contain family detail, but are **not separately indexed online** — must be requested from NARA.

### 📊 Census Records
- **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** — One of the few surviving 1890-era censuses nationally (the regular 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire). Held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society**.
- **1900 Federal Census** — The first regular federal census to include the area.
- **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** (FamilySearch collection 1987432) — Relevant if the family has any Indian Territory connections.

### 🏥 Vital Records
- Oklahoma Territory had **no statewide civil registration** at the time of the Run. Treat any statewide registration-start dates as unconfirmed until verified directly on the FamilySearch Wiki.

### ⛪ Church Records
- Church records begin sporadically from 1889, as denominations established congregations in newly opened towns.
- FamilySearch — "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321).

### ⚖️ Court Records
- District court civil, criminal, probate, and naturalization records for Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) are held at:
  - **National Archives at Fort Worth**
  - **Oklahoma State Archives**

### 💍 Marriage Records
- FamilySearch — "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (collection 2134789, begins the year after the run, county-level once counties organized).

### 🪶 Native American Enrollment
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910 — digitized on FamilySearch but **browse-only (0% indexed)**, must be paged through image by image.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives (Washington D.C.) | GLO homestead case files (RG 49) | archives.gov / in-person |
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Oklahoma Territory district court records | In-person / written request |
| BLM GLO Records | Homestead patents index | glorecords.blm.gov (free) |
| Oklahoma Historical Society | 1890 territorial special census; territorial records | In-person / written request |
| FamilySearch | Land records, Indian rolls, marriages, church records, digitized volumes | Free online |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (1900+) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Land-run-era newspapers, marriage/obituary notices | Subscription |

---

## Research Tips
1. **Read the full homestead file**, not just the patent — witness affidavits in GLO case files often name neighbors and relatives.
2. **Prioritize the 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census** (Oklahoma Historical Society) — it's a rare survivor and fills the gap left by the destroyed national 1890 census.
3. **Search departure states** — Many settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and nearby states. Search those states' land, church, and county records for years just before 1889.
4. Church records in new Land Run towns are thin immediately after 1889 — don't expect complete parish coverage for that year.
5. Because Oklahoma didn't become a state until 1907, some standard state-level online pages (such as vital records guides) cover only the statehood period — verify territorial-era coverage directly on the FamilySearch Wiki.

---

**Next step:** Share a specific ancestor's name, approximate birth year, and any county or township you have — that will allow a focused search in the homestead, census, or court records described above.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, pre-statehood (Mississippi Territory / Alabama Territory, c. 1798–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** The present-day Alabama region was part of the **Mississippi Territory** from 1798 to 1817, then split off as the **Alabama Territory** from 1817 until statehood in 1819. No standalone "Alabama" jurisdiction existed around 1800.
- **Earlier colonial control:** The Mobile area was successively administered by France (1702–1763), Britain (1763–1780), and Spain (1780–1813).
- **Key events:** The Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. Major Carolina/Virginia/Georgia migration followed the Creek War of 1813–1814.

## Boundary Changes

| Period | Jurisdiction |
|---|---|
| Before 1798 | French, then British, then Spanish colonial territory (Mobile District) |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory |
| 1819 onward | State of Alabama |

**Research implication:** Search under both "Mississippi Territory" *and* "Alabama/Alabama Territory." FamilySearch often files territorial-era material under the modern state name.

---

## Available Record Types
